title: A quarrel over an ass’s shadow
english: In the first book of our reply to Celsus’s boastful title (for he entitled the book he composed against us The True Doctrine), we dealt, as you instructed, most faithful Ambrose, and as far as we were able, with his preface, and then tested each of his statements in turn, until we ended with the speech of the Jew that he has invented against Jesus. In the second book we met, as best we could, every point in the speech that his Jew makes against us who believe in God through Christ. Now we begin this third book, in which our task is to contend with what he sets out in his own person.

He says that “Christians and Jews quarrel with one another most foolishly,” and he says that our debate with one another about Christ is no different from what the proverb calls “a fight over the shadow of an ass.” He thinks there is nothing worthy of respect in the inquiry that Jews and Christians carry on with one another, since both believe that it was prophesied by a divine Spirit that a Saviour would come to dwell among the human race, but beyond that they do not agree on whether the one prophesied has come or not.

For we Christians have believed in Jesus as the one who came in accordance with the prophecies. But most of the Jews are so far from believing in him that those of that time plotted against Jesus, and those of the present day, approving what the Jews then dared against him, speak evil of Jesus, as though by some sorcery he had pretended to be the one whose coming the prophets proclaimed, who is called Christ in the ancestral usage of the Jews.

title: A people without gods needed prophets
english: Let Celsus, then, and those who are pleased with what he says against us, tell us whether it is like the shadow of an ass that the prophets of the Jews foretold the birthplace of him who would lead those who have lived good lives and those who are called God’s portion (Micah 5:2; Matthew 2:6; Deuteronomy 32:9); that a virgin would conceive Emmanuel (Isaiah 7:14); that such signs and wonders would be done by the one prophesied; that “his word will run swiftly” (Psalm 147:15), so that the voice of his apostles went out “into all the earth” (Psalm 19:4; Romans 10:18); and what he would suffer when condemned by the Jews, and how he would rise again.

Did the prophets say these things at random, with no convincing reason to move them not only to speak but also to judge their words worthy of being written down? And did so great a nation as the Jews, which long ago received a land of its own to dwell in, with no convincing reason proclaim some men as prophets and reject others as false prophets? Was there nothing among them that moved them to number the words of the later men who were held to be prophets with the books of Moses, which were believed to be sacred?

And can those who accuse Jews and Christians of foolishness show us that the nation of the Jews could have held together if there had been no promise of foreknowledge among them? Can they show that, while the nations around them each believed, according to their ancestral customs, that they received oracles and divinations from those they held to be gods, these alone, who had been taught to despise all the gods held by the nations as being not gods but demons (for their prophets said, “All the gods of the nations are demons” (Psalm 96:5)), had no one who professed to prophesy and who could hold back those who, out of longing to know the future beforehand, wished to desert to the demons of the other peoples?

Consider, then, whether it was not necessary that a whole nation taught to despise the gods of the other peoples should have had an abundance of prophets, who by that very fact showed something greater, surpassing the oracles found everywhere.

title: Wonders among the Jews and the Spirit in the prophets
english: Again: were mighty works done everywhere, or in many places (as Celsus himself relates further on, telling of Asclepius doing good and foretelling the future to whole cities dedicated to him, such as Tricca, Epidaurus, Cos and Pergamum, and of Aristeas of Proconnesus, a certain man of Clazomenae, and Cleomedes of Astypalaea), while among the Jews alone, who say they are dedicated to the God of the universe, there was no sign or wonder to support and confirm their faith in the Creator of the universe, together with their hope of another and greater life? How could that be? They would at once have gone over to worshipping the demons who give oracles and heal, and abandoned the God whom they believed to help them, though only in word, and who never showed his presence at all.

But if this did not happen, and they even endured countless sufferings so as not to renounce Judaism and the law that belongs to it, suffering at one time in Assyria, at another in Persia, at another under Antiochus, is it not shown from probability, to those who disbelieve the extraordinary histories and prophecies, that such things were not fictions, but that a divine Spirit, dwelling in the souls of the prophets as in pure souls, for they were men who had taken on every toil for the sake of virtue, moved them to prophesy some things to their own contemporaries, others to those who came later, and above all concerning a Saviour who would come to dwell among the human race?

title: Seeking the promised one is no trifle
english: If this is so, how are Jews and Christians disputing with one another over the shadow of an ass, when they examine, from the prophecies in which both alike believe, whether the one prophesied has come, or has not yet come at all and is still awaited? And even if, for argument’s sake, Celsus were granted that Jesus is not the one whom the prophets announced, even so, the inquiry into the meaning of the prophetic Scriptures is still no dispute over the shadow of an ass. Its aim is that the one proclaimed beforehand may be clearly shown: what sort of person he was prophesied to be, what he would do, and, if possible, when he would come.

We have already spoken earlier about Jesus being the prophesied Christ, setting out a few prophecies out of many. Neither Jews nor Christians, then, are mistaken in accepting that the prophets spoke from God. But those who are mistaken about the one prophesied and awaited hold a false opinion about who he is and what kind of person he was proclaimed to be in the true word of the prophets.

title: Celsus’s tale of a revolt from Egypt
english: Next, Celsus supposes that the Jews, being Egyptians by race, left Egypt after rising in revolt against the Egyptian commonwealth and scorning the religious customs of Egypt. He says that what they did to the Egyptians they have suffered at the hands of those who joined Jesus and believed in him as Christ, and that in both cases the cause of the new movement was revolt against the commonwealth.

We must consider what Celsus has done here. The Egyptians of old treated the race of the Hebrews badly in many ways (Exodus 1:11–14), after the Hebrews had come to dwell in Egypt because of a famine that had seized Judaea (Genesis 47:4). For wronging strangers and suppliants they suffered what a whole nation was bound to suffer at the hands of divine providence, since it had conspired against the whole race of its guests, who had done it no wrong. Struck by scourges from God, they let go, grudgingly, though before long, those whom they were unjustly holding in slavery, to go wherever they wished (Exodus 12:31–32).

Since, then, the Egyptians love themselves and prefer their own countrymen, whatever they are like, even to foreigners who are more just, there is no accusation they have failed to make against Moses and the Hebrews. They do not altogether deny the wonderful works done through Moses, but they say these were done by sorcery and not by divine power. Moses, however, being no sorcerer but a devout man, dedicated to the God of the universe and sharing in a more divine spirit, both laid down laws for the Hebrews as God prompted him and recorded what had happened just as it truly was.

title: The Hebrew language disproves the revolt
english: Celsus, then, did not act as a fair examiner of the story as the Egyptians tell it one way and the Hebrews another. Prejudiced beforehand in favour of the Egyptians, as though they were dearer to him, he accepted as true the account of those who wronged the strangers, and said that the Hebrews, who had been wronged, left Egypt in revolt. He did not see that so great a rebellious multitude of Egyptians, whose beginning was revolt, could not, at the very moment of revolting, have become a nation and changed its language as well, so that those who until then had used the Egyptian tongue should suddenly have full command of the Hebrew language.

But suppose, for argument’s sake, that when they left Egypt they also came to hate the language they had grown up with. Why then did they not afterwards use the language of the Syrians or of the Phoenicians, rather than establish Hebrew, a language different from both? What my argument means to show is this: it is false that certain people who were Egyptians by race revolted against the Egyptians, left Egypt, came to Palestine and settled in what is now called Judaea. For the Hebrews had an ancestral language before they went down into Egypt, and there were Hebrew letters, different from those of the Egyptians, which Moses used to write the five books that the Jews believe to be sacred.

title: Christians never began in revolt
english: It is likewise false that the Hebrews, being Egyptians, had their beginning in a revolt, and false that, in the time of Jesus, others who were Jews revolted against the Jewish commonwealth and followed Jesus. For neither Celsus nor those who think as he does will be able to point to any act of revolt on the part of the Christians.

And yet, if revolt had been the cause of the Christians’ coming together (and they took their beginning from the Jews, who were permitted both to take up arms in defence of their own and to kill their enemies), the lawgiver of the Christians would not have forbidden the killing of a human being altogether, never teaching that any assault by his disciples on another man is just, even if that man is utterly unjust (for he did not think it fitting for his divine legislation to allow the killing of any human being whatever). Nor would Christians, if they had begun from revolt, have accepted laws so exceedingly gentle, under which it was their lot to be slain “like sheep” (Psalm 44:22; Romans 8:36) and never to be able to defend themselves against those who persecuted them.

Moreover, if one examines the matter more deeply, one may say of those who came out of the land of Egypt that the whole people, beyond all expectation, took up all at once the language called Hebrew, as though it were a gift from God. As one of their own prophets said, “When they came out of the land of Egypt, he heard a language he did not know” (Psalm 81:5).

title: Hebrew names, and God’s care for the Christians
english: That those who left Egypt with Moses were not Egyptians may also be argued in this way. If they had been Egyptians, their names ought to have been Egyptian, since in every language the names belong to that language. But if it is clear from their names, which are Hebrew, that they were not Egyptians (for Scripture is full of Hebrew names, and of people in Egypt who gave such names to their sons), then the Egyptians’ claim that they were Egyptians driven out of Egypt with Moses is plainly false. And it is quite evident that, being descended from Hebrew ancestors according to the history recorded by Moses, they used their own language, from which they also named their sons.

As for the Christians: because they were taught not to defend themselves against their enemies, and kept the gentle and humane legislation, they have received from God what they would not have accomplished had they been given leave to make war, even if they had been very powerful: from God, who has always fought for them, and from time to time has stopped those who rose up against the Christians and wished to kill them.

For as a reminder, so that by looking upon a few contending for godliness they might be of more proven worth and despise death, a few at various times, and very easily counted, have died for the Christian worship of God, while God prevented their whole nation from being wiped out by war. For he willed that it should be established, and that the whole earth should be filled with this saving and most godly teaching. And again, so that the weaker might have respite from their anxiety about death, God provided for those who believe, scattering every plot against them by his will alone, so that neither kings nor local governors nor the populace could be inflamed against them any further.
So much in answer to what Celsus said: that revolt was the beginning, long ago, of the Jews’ coming together as a people, and later of the Christians’ coming into being.

title: Christians want everyone to believe
english: In what follows he plainly lies, so let us also set out his very words. He says: “If all men should wish to be Christians, these people would no longer wish it.”

That this is false is clear from the fact that Christians, so far as it rests with them, do not neglect to sow the word in every part of the world. Some, indeed, have made it their work to travel round not only cities but also villages and farmsteads, so as to make others, too, devout toward God. And no one could say that they do this for the sake of wealth. Sometimes they do not even accept what they need for food; and if ever want of it forces them to accept it, they are content with what they need and no more, even when more people are willing to share with them and to give them more than they need.

Now, perhaps, when because of the great number who come to the word even the rich, and some people of rank, and refined and well-born women welcome those who preach the word, someone will dare to say that some become leaders in the Christian teaching for the sake of a little glory. But at the beginning, when the danger was great, above all for those who taught, no one could reasonably suspect any such thing. And even now the ill repute they have among everyone else is greater than the supposed glory they have among those who share their belief, and not all of them have even that. So it is false on its face that “if all men should wish to be Christians, these people would no longer wish it.”

title: Few at first, but never few
english: See also what he says is the proof of this. “When they were beginning,” he says, “they were few and of one mind; but once they had spread into a multitude, they are cut apart and split again, and each group wants factions of its own; for this is what they wanted from the start.”

That the Christians were few at the beginning, compared with the multitude that came after, is clear. Yet they were not altogether few. For what stirred up envy against Jesus and roused the Jews to plot against him was the great number of those who followed him into the deserts: five thousand men followed him, and four thousand, not counting the women and children (Matthew 14:21; Matthew 15:38). Such was the charm in the words of Jesus that not only men wished to follow him into the wilderness, but women too, who let neither their womanly weakness nor what people might think of their following the teacher into the wilderness hold them back. Children too, wholly free from passion, followed with their parents, either going after those who had begotten them, or perhaps also led by his divinity, so that divinity might be sown in them.
But let it be granted that they were few at the beginning. How does this help to show that Christians would not wish to persuade all men of the word?

title: Disagreements from the very beginning
english: He also says that they all “were of one mind,” not seeing even here that from the beginning there were disagreements among believers over the interpretation of the books believed to be divine. At any rate, while the apostles were still preaching and the eyewitnesses of Jesus were teaching what he had taught, the believers from among the Jews had no small debate with one another (Acts 15:1–7) about the Gentiles who were coming over to the word: whether they must keep the Jewish customs, or whether the “burden” (Acts 15:28) of clean and unclean foods should be lifted, as not required, from the Gentiles who had left their ancestral ways and believed in Jesus.

Moreover, in the letters of Paul, who lived in the time of those who had seen Jesus, we find things said that show that questions had been raised about the resurrection, and about its having “already taken place” (2 Timothy 2:18), and about the day of the Lord, whether it “has come” or not (2 Thessalonians 2:2). And again the saying, “turning away from the profane empty talk and the contradictions of what is falsely called knowledge, which some have professed, and so made shipwreck of the faith” (1 Timothy 6:20–21; 1 Timothy 1:19), shows that some misreadings arose from the beginning, and not, as Celsus supposes, only after believers had become many.

title: Serious things breed sects
english: Then, as if bringing a charge against the word, he reproaches us with the sects within Christianity, saying: “But once they had spread into a multitude, they split and are cut apart again, and each group wants factions of its own.” And he says that “being divided again because of their numbers, they refute one another; they still have, so to speak, one thing in common, if indeed they have even that: the name; and this alone they are nevertheless ashamed to abandon; in everything else they are ranged one here, another there.”

To this too we shall say that differing sects have never arisen in any matter unless its first principle is serious and useful to life. Since medicine is useful and necessary to the human race, and many questions are raised in it about how bodies should be treated, for this reason there are admittedly many sects in medicine among the Greeks, and I think also among the barbarians, at least among all who profess to practise medicine. Again, since philosophy professes truth and the knowledge of things that are, lays down how one ought to live, and tries to teach what benefits our race, while the matters it inquires into allow wide differences of view, for this reason a great many sects have arisen in philosophy, some more famous, others less so. And Judaism too found occasion for sects to arise in the differing interpretation of the writings of Moses and the words of the prophets.

So then, since Christianity appeared to people as something worthy of reverence, not only, as Celsus supposes, to the more slavish, but also to many of the learned among the Greeks, sects necessarily arose, not altogether because of factions and love of strife, but because a number of the learned too were eager to understand the teachings of Christianity. From this it followed that, as they interpreted differently the words that all alike believed to be divine, sects arose named after men who admired the first principle of the word, yet were moved somehow by certain plausible arguments to their disagreements with one another.

But no one could reasonably shun medicine because of the sects within it, nor would anyone who aims at what is fitting hate philosophy, using its many sects as a pretext for hating it. So neither should the sacred books of Moses and the prophets be condemned because of the sects among the Jews.

title: Sects show who is approved
english: If this reasoning holds, why should we not make the same defence for the sects among Christians as well? Of these, Paul seems to me to have spoken most admirably: “For there must also be sects among you, so that those who are approved may become manifest among you” (1 Corinthians 11:19). For the man approved in medicine is the one who, having trained himself in various sects and fairly examined most of them, has chosen the best; and the man who makes great progress in philosophy is the one who, having come to know more of them, has trained himself in them and attached himself to the argument that prevailed. In the same way I would say that one who has looked carefully into the sects of Judaism and of Christianity becomes a most wise Christian.

But anyone who accuses the word because of the sects would also accuse the teaching of Socrates, from whose school there have come many schools of men who do not think alike. One might also accuse Plato’s doctrines because of Aristotle, who broke away from his school by introducing new ideas; we have spoken of him earlier too.

Celsus, it seems to me, knew of some sects that do not even share the name of Jesus with us. Perhaps he had heard talk of the so-called Ophites and Cainites, and of any other such school of thought that has arisen by breaking away from Jesus entirely. But this does nothing to show that the teaching of Christians is open to accusation.

title: Our union comes from God
english: After this he says: “Their union is all the more wonderful, the more it can be shown to have been formed on no adequate basis. But there is an adequate basis: faction, the advantage it brings, and fear of outsiders; these things make their faith firm.”

To this too we shall say that our union rests on a basis of such a kind, or rather not on a basis at all but on God’s working, that its origin is God, who taught people through the prophets to hope for the coming of Christ, who would save them. For in so far as this is not truly refuted, even if unbelievers seem to refute it, so far the word is established as the word of God, and Jesus is shown to be the Son of God both before he became man and when he had become man.

And I say that even after he became man he is always found, by those who have the keenest eyes of the soul, to be most worthy of God and truly come down to us from God; and that he has neither his origin nor what followed his origin from human understanding, but from the manifestation of God, who by manifold wisdom and manifold powers established first Judaism and after it Christianity. The view has also been refuted that faction, and the advantage gained through faction, are the origin of the word that has converted so many people and made them better.

title: Not held together by fear
english: That “fear of outsiders” does not hold our union together either is clear from this: by God’s will, that fear too has already been at an end for a good while now. And it is likely that the freedom from fear, as regards this life, that believers have come to enjoy will come to an end, whenever those who slander the word in every way come again to think that the cause of the faction, now so great among the multitude of believers, lies in their not being warred upon by the rulers as in former times. For we have learned from the word neither to grow slack in peace and give ourselves up to ease, nor, when the world wars against us, to lose heart and fall away from our love for the God of the universe in Jesus Christ (Romans 8:39).

So we set forth the dignity of our origin plainly, and do not, as Celsus thinks, hide it, when even in those who are only beginning instruction we instil contempt for idols and for all statues, and besides this, raising their thoughts from serving created things instead of God (Romans 1:25), we lift them up to the one who created all things. And we clearly present the one who was prophesied, both from the prophecies about him (and these are many) and from the Gospels and the words of the apostles, as these are handed on with precision to those able to hear with more understanding.

title: What terrors do we invent?
english: What are these “all sorts of things” by which we draw people, or what are the “terrors” we “invent,” as Celsus writes without any proof? Let anyone who wishes show it. Unless, perhaps, Celsus means to call “invented terrors” the teaching about God as judge and about men being judged for all they have done, a teaching established with varied proof, partly from the Scriptures and partly from reasonable argument.

And yet (for truth is dear) Celsus says, near the end of his work, “May neither these people, nor I, nor any other human being cast off the doctrine that the unjust will be punished and the just counted worthy of rewards.” What terrors, then, if you take away the teaching on punishment, do we invent to draw people in?

Again, when he says that we invent “misheard versions of the ancient account” and with these pipe to people beforehand and fill their ears beforehand, “like those who make a din around people in the frenzy of the Corybantic rites,” we shall say to him: misheard versions of what ancient account? For whether it is the Greek account, which also taught about the courts beneath the earth, or the Jewish one, which among other things prophesied also about the life that follows this life, he could not show that we live by such doctrines as men who have misheard the truth, at least those of us who try to believe with reason.

title: Egyptian temples and the Christian faith
english: He wants to compare the things of our faith with the practices of the Egyptians. Among them, as one approaches, there are splendid sacred precincts and groves, great and beautiful gateways, wonderful temples, magnificent pavilions all around, and rites deeply devout and full of mystery; but once one has gone in and further inside, what one sees being worshipped is a cat, or an ape, or a crocodile, or a goat, or a dog.

What, then, is there among us that corresponds to the things of the Egyptians that look solemn to those approaching, and what corresponds to the irrational animals worshipped inside, beyond the solemn gateways? Or are the prophecies, the God over all, and the teaching against images the things that even he counts solemn, while Jesus Christ crucified corresponds to the irrational animal that is worshipped? If he says this (and I do not think he will say anything else), we will answer that a good deal has already been said by us above in support of what concerns Jesus: that even what seems to have befallen him as a man has come about for the good of the universe and for the salvation of the whole world.

title: Egyptian symbols and the gifts of the Spirit
english: Then he says that the things of the Egyptians, who speak with solemnity even about the irrational animals and claim that they are in some way symbols of a god, or whatever those who are styled their prophets like to call them, give those who have learned these things the impression that they were not initiated in vain.

But as for the things in our teaching that are presented to the deeply learned in Christianity from what Paul calls a gift, in the “word of wisdom” given “through the Spirit” and in the “word of knowledge” given “according to the Spirit” (1 Corinthians 12:8), Celsus does not seem to me even to have imagined them. I judge this not only from these remarks but also from what he says later, when he accuses the Christian body of driving every wise man away from the teaching of their faith and inviting only the senseless and the slavish. We shall see about this in due course, when we reach that passage.

title: Riddles of Egypt and the wisdom of Paul
english: He also says that we laugh at the Egyptians, although they offer many riddles that are far from contemptible, when they teach that such practices are honours paid to eternal ideas and not, as most people think, to creatures that live for a day; but that we are simpletons, bringing into our narratives about Jesus nothing more solemn than the goats and dogs of the Egyptians.

To this too we will say: My good sir, are you right to extol the Egyptians in your discourse for offering many riddles that are far from contemptible, and obscure narratives about the animals among them, and yet wrong to accuse us, as though you were convinced that we say nothing of substance, and that everything we say is worthless and contemptible, when we set out the things concerning Jesus according to the wisdom of the word to those who are, as it were, mature in Christianity? It is of these, as people fit to hear the wisdom that is in Christianity, that Paul teaches when he says: “We speak wisdom among the mature, yet a wisdom not of this age, nor of the rulers of this age, who are being brought to nothing; but we speak God’s wisdom in a mystery, the hidden wisdom, which God foreordained before the ages for our glory, which none of the rulers of this age has known” (1 Corinthians 2:6–8).

title: A challenge to read Paul's letters
english: And we say to those who share Celsus’s mind: Did Paul, then, imagine no surpassing wisdom when he promised to speak “wisdom among the mature” (1 Corinthians 2:6)? And when, in keeping with his audacity, he says that Paul made these promises though he had nothing wise, we will answer him: First explain the letters of the man who says this. Look closely into the meaning of each expression in them, for example in the letter to the Ephesians, and to the Colossians, and to the Thessalonians, and to the Philippians, and to the Romans, and show two things: that you have understood Paul’s words, and that you can prove some of them simple-minded or silly.

For if he gives himself to reading them with attention, I know well that either he will admire the mind of the man, who conceives great things in plain language, or, if he does not admire it, he will himself appear ridiculous, whether he explains the man’s meaning as though he had understood it, or tries to contradict and overturn what he imagined Paul had in mind.

title: The hidden depths of the Gospels
english: And I say nothing yet of the close study of everything written in the Gospels, each part of which holds a meaning that is large and hard to discern, not only for the many but even for some of the intelligent. That meaning contains a most profound explanation of the parables, which Jesus spoke to “those outside” (Mark 4:11), while he kept their clear sense for those who had passed beyond outward hearing and came to him privately (Mark 4:34) “in the house” (Matthew 13:36). And he will marvel when he understands why some are called “outside” and others “in the house.”

And again, who among those able to see would not be struck with wonder at Jesus’ movements: going up a mountain for certain words (Matthew 5:1), or deeds, or for his own transfiguration (Matthew 17:1–2), and below healing those who were sick and unable to go up where his disciples follow him (Matthew 17:14–18)? But now is not the time to set out what is truly solemn and divine in the Gospels, or the mind of Christ in Paul (1 Corinthians 2:16), that is, of Wisdom (1 Corinthians 1:24) and of the Word. But even these remarks are enough against the unphilosophical mockery of Celsus, who likens the inner and mystical things of the Church of God to the cats, or apes, or crocodiles, or goats, or dogs of the Egyptians.

title: Men the Greeks made into gods
english: Omitting no kind of disparagement and ridicule of us, the buffoon Celsus, in his discourse against us, names the Dioscuri, Heracles, Asclepius, and Dionysus, who are believed among the Greeks to have become gods after being men. And he says that we cannot bear to regard these as gods, because they were men to begin with, although they displayed many noble deeds on behalf of mankind; whereas we, he says, claim that Jesus, after he died, was seen by his own devotees. He further accuses us of saying that he was seen, and that, too, as a shadow.

To this too we will say that Celsus has craftily neither stated clearly that he does not worship these as gods (for he was wary of the opinion of those who would read his writing, who would take him for an atheist if he championed anything of the truth as it appeared to him), nor, on the other hand, pretended that he himself regards them as gods; for we would have replied to either position.

Come, then, let us say this to those who do not regard them as gods. Do these men not exist at all, their soul too having perished, as some think the human soul perishes at once? Or, according to the opinion of those who say that the soul survives or is immortal, do these survive or are they immortal, being not gods but heroes? Or are they not even heroes, but simply souls? If, then, you suppose that they do not exist, we must establish our primary doctrine about the soul; but if they do exist, then here too the doctrine of immortality must be accepted, not only from those Greeks who spoke well about it, but also in accordance with what the divine teachings hold.

And we will show that these men, who worshipped many gods, cannot have come to a better place and portion after their departure from this world. We will bring forward the stories about them, in which are recorded the great licentiousness of Heracles and his womanish slavery to Omphale, and how Asclepius was struck by a thunderbolt from their Zeus. The story of the Dioscuri will also be told, that “now they live on alternate days, and now again they are dead; and they have won honour equal to the gods” (Homer, Odyssey 11.303–304), they who die over and over. How then do they think it reasonable that any of these should be regarded as a god or a hero?

title: The stories of the heroes set beside the story of Jesus
english: But we, after showing from the prophetic writings what concerns our Jesus, and then comparing the history about him with the histories about them, [ … ] that no licentiousness is recorded of him. For not even those who plotted against him and sought “false testimony” against him (Matthew 26:59) found so much as a plausible ground for their “false testimony,” so as to accuse him of licentiousness. What is more, his death came about through a plot of men, and had nothing like the thunderbolt that struck Asclepius. And what is there that is solemn about the frenzied Dionysus, dressed in women’s clothing, that he should be worshipped as a god? And if those who defend these figures take refuge in allegories, we must examine separately whether the allegories are sound, and separately whether those who are torn apart by Titans and cast down from the heavenly throne can have real existence and be worthy of reverence and worship.

But our Jesus, who was seen by his own “devotees” (for I will use the word found in Celsus), was seen in truth; and Celsus slanders our message when he says that he was seen as a shadow. Let the histories about those figures be examined alongside the history of Jesus. Or does Celsus want those to be true, but these to be fictions, though they were written down by eyewitnesses, who showed by their deeds how clearly they had grasped what they had beheld, and who displayed their disposition by what they eagerly suffered for his message? And who, wishing to act in everything according to reason, would arbitrarily assent to the stories about those figures, while rushing at the accounts about this one without examination and disbelieving what is told of him?

title: Witnesses to Asclepius and witnesses to Jesus
english: And again, when it is said of Asclepius that a great multitude of people, Greeks and barbarians alike, declare that they have often seen him and still see him, not as a mere apparition, but healing, doing good, and foretelling the future, Celsus thinks it right that we believe it, and does not find fault with the believers in Jesus when we believe these things. But when we assent to the disciples, who both beheld the wonders of Jesus and clearly show the good faith of their conscience, because we see their freedom from guile, so far as one can see a conscience from writings, Celsus calls us simpletons, though he cannot produce the “countless multitude,” as he says, of Greeks and barbarians who acknowledge Asclepius.

For our part, if he thinks this impressive, we clearly show a countless multitude of Greeks and barbarians who acknowledge Jesus. And some display signs that they have received something more wonderful through this faith, in the cures they perform, invoking over those who need healing nothing other than the God over all and the name of Jesus together with the history about him. For by these means we too have seen many set free from grievous afflictions, from derangements and madness, and from countless other ills, which neither men nor demons had healed.

title: Healing and prophecy do not prove a god
english: Even if I grant that a certain demon who is a physician, the one called Asclepius, heals bodies, I would say to those who marvel at such a thing, or at the prophecy of Apollo: if the healing of bodies is a morally indifferent thing, something that falls to the lot not only of the good but also of the wicked, and if foreknowledge of the future is also indifferent (for the one who foreknows does not necessarily display goodness), then show how those who heal or foreknow are in no way wicked, but are proved by every means to be good, and not far from being thought gods. But they will not be able to prove that those who heal or foreknow are good, since many are said to be healed who are unworthy even to live, whom the wise man, were he a physician, would never have wished to heal, since they live as they ought not.

In the oracles of the Pythian god, too, you would find some commands that are not reasonable. I shall set out two of them for the present. He ordered that Cleomedes, the boxer, I think, be honoured with honours equal to a god's. I do not know what he saw that was so venerable in his boxing; yet he did not honour Pythagoras or Socrates with the honours of the boxer. Again, by calling Archilochus a "servant of the Muses", a man who displayed his poetic art on the vilest and most licentious subject matter and showed a licentious and impure character, he proclaimed him a pious man, in so far as he was a "servant of the Muses", who are reputed to be gods. I do not know whether even an ordinary person would say that the pious man is not adorned with every kind of moderation and virtue, or whether a decent man would say the sort of things contained in the unseemly iambics of Archilochus.

If nothing divine shows itself on its face in the medicine of Asclepius and the prophecy of Apollo, how could anyone reasonably worship them as gods, as pure beings, even if I grant that these things are so? Above all when, through the Pythian vent, the prophetic spirit, Apollo, the one pure of an earthly body, steals into the so-called prophetess through her female parts as she sits over it? We hold no such opinion about Jesus and his power. For the body born of the virgin was made up of human matter, open to human wounds and to death.

title: Celsus tells the story of Aristeas
english: Let us see also what Celsus says after this, as he sets out marvels from the histories which in themselves look incredible, yet which he does not disbelieve, at least so far as his words go. First comes the story of Aristeas of Proconnesus, about whom he says this: "Then Aristeas of Proconnesus: he vanished from among men in so supernatural a way, appeared again plainly, long afterwards visited many parts of the world and reported marvels, and Apollo enjoined the Metapontines to count Aristeas among the gods; yet no one any longer regards this man as a god."

He seems to have taken the story from Pindar and Herodotus. For now it is enough to set out the words of Herodotus from the fourth book of his Histories, which run thus about him (Herodotus, Histories 4.14–15): "Where Aristeas, who said these things, came from, I have told; and the account I heard of him in Proconnesus and Cyzicus I shall tell. They say that Aristeas, who was inferior in birth to none of the citizens, went into a fuller's shop in Proconnesus and died there, and that the fuller locked up his workshop and went off to tell the dead man's relatives. When the report that Aristeas was dead had already spread through the city, a man of Cyzicus who had come from the town of Artace disputed it with those who were saying it, declaring that he had met Aristeas as he was going toward Cyzicus and had spoken with him. While he was disputing it hotly, the dead man's relatives came to the fuller's shop with what was needed to take up the body; but when the room was opened, Aristeas was to be seen neither alive nor dead. In the seventh year afterwards he appeared in Proconnesus and composed the verses which the Greeks now call the Arimaspea, and having composed them he vanished a second time.

"This is what these cities say. But this I know happened to the Metapontines in Italy two hundred and forty years after the second disappearance of Aristeas, as I found by reckoning in Proconnesus and in Metapontum. The Metapontines say that Aristeas himself appeared to them in their country and bade them set up an altar to Apollo, and beside it a statue bearing the name of Aristeas of Proconnesus. For he told them that theirs was the only country of all the Italian Greeks to which Apollo had come, and that he himself, who was now Aristeas, was following him; but at that time, when he followed the god, he was a raven. Having said this he vanished; and the Metapontines say that they sent to Delphi and asked the god what the apparition of the man might be. The Pythia bade them obey the apparition, saying that if they obeyed, it would go better for them. They accepted this and carried it out. And to this day there stands a statue bearing the name of Aristeas beside the very image of Apollo, with laurels around it; the image is set up in the marketplace. So much, then, for Aristeas."

title: Why believe Herodotus and not the disciples?
english: To the story about Aristeas we must say this. If Celsus had set it out as a story, without also showing his own assent as one who had accepted it as true, we would have met his argument in another way. But he says that Aristeas vanished in a supernatural way, appeared again plainly, visited many parts of the world and reported marvels; and he also sets out the oracle of Apollo, who enjoined the Metapontines to count Aristeas among the gods, in his own voice and with assent. So we address our reply to him: How is it that you take the marvels recorded about Jesus by his disciples to be sheer fictions, and blame those who believe them, yet do not consider these stories either tall tales or fictions? And how is it that you, who accuse others of believing the marvels about Jesus without reason, show that you have believed so many such things yourself, bringing no proof about them and no argument that they happened? Or are Herodotus and Pindar held by you to be free of falsehood, while those who trained themselves to die for the teachings of Jesus, and who left to those after them such writings about the things they were convinced of, contend so hard for what you think are fictions, myths and tall tales that for their sake they live amid hardships and die by violence?

Place yourself, then, midway between what is written about Aristeas and what is related about Jesus, and see whether, from the outcome and from those who are helped to amend their characters and to revere the God over all, it is not possible to say that we must believe the things related about Jesus, as things that did not happen without God, but not the things about Aristeas of Proconnesus.

title: The purpose behind the wonders of Jesus
english: For what purpose did providence work the marvels about Aristeas, and what benefit did it mean to bring to the human race by displaying things as great as you think these were? You cannot say. But when we tell the story of Jesus, we offer no ordinary defence for these things having happened: namely, that God willed to commend as saving for men the message that came through Jesus. That message was made firm through the apostles, as it were the foundations of the building of Christianity that was being laid (Ephesians 2:20), and it has grown in later times too, in which not a few healings are performed in the name of Jesus, along with certain other manifestations that are not to be despised.

And what sort of being is Apollo, who enjoins the Metapontines to count Aristeas among the gods? With what purpose does he do this, and what benefit is he arranging for the Metapontines from honouring Aristeas as a god, if they should now reckon as a god one who a little before was a man? Yet the commendations of Aristeas by Apollo, who in our view is a demon that has received as his privilege "libation and the savour of sacrifice" (Homer, Iliad 4.49), seem to you worth mention; while the commendations from the God over all and his holy angels, foretold through prophets not after Jesus had come but before he came to dwell in human life, do not move you to marvel both at the prophets who received the divine Spirit and at the one whom they prophesied?

It came about that his coming into this life was proclaimed many years beforehand, and by so many, that the whole nation of the Jews, hanging on the expectation of the one they hoped would come, fell to debating among themselves when Jesus came. A great multitude of them confessed him as Christ and believed that he was the one prophesied. But those who did not believe despised the meekness of those who, because of the teachings of Jesus, would not stir up strife even in the least, and dared to do against Jesus such things as his disciples recorded with love of truth and candour, not stealthily removing from the wonderful story about him what seems to most people to bring shame on the Christians' message.

For both Jesus himself and his disciples wished those who came to them to believe not only in his divinity and his marvels, as if he had not shared in human nature or taken on the flesh which in human beings "desires against the spirit" (Galatians 5:17). But they saw too that the power which came down into human nature and human circumstances, and took on a human soul and body, contributes by being believed, together with the more divine things, to the salvation of those who believe, who see that from him the divine and human natures began to be woven together, so that the human, by fellowship with what is more divine, might become divine, not in Jesus alone but also in all who, along with believing, take up the life which Jesus taught, the life that leads everyone who lives by the precepts of Jesus to friendship with God and fellowship with him.

title: The churches of God shine like lights
english: So Apollo, as Celsus tells it, wants the Metapontines to count Aristeas among the gods. But since the Metapontines thought the plain evidence about Aristeas, a man and perhaps not a good one, stronger than the oracle that called him a god or worthy of divine honours, they were not willing to obey Apollo; and so no one regards Aristeas as a god.

About Jesus we would say this. It was to the advantage of the human race to receive him as Son of God, God come in a human soul and body; and this did not seem profitable to the gluttony of the body-loving demons or of those who think them gods. For this reason the demons on earth, who are thought to be gods by those not instructed about demons, and also those who serve them, wanted to hinder the spread of the teaching of Jesus. For they saw that the libations and the savour of sacrifices, in which they greedily took pleasure, were being done away with as the teachings of Jesus prevailed. But God, who sent Jesus, brought to nothing all the plotting of the demons, and made the gospel of Jesus prevail in every part of the world for the conversion and amendment of human beings, and made churches arise everywhere that live as a rival commonwealth to the assemblies of the superstitious, the licentious and the unjust. For such are the crowds that everywhere act as citizens in the assemblies of the cities. But the churches of God that have been made disciples of Christ, when compared with the assemblies of the peoples among whom they dwell as sojourners, are "like lights in the world" (Philippians 2:15). For who would not admit that even the worse members of the church, and those who fall short by comparison with the better, are much better than the assemblies of the peoples?

title: The Church beside the city assembly
english: For the church of God at Athens, let us say, is a gentle and steady body, since it wishes to please the God over all; but the assembly of the Athenians is given to faction and can in no way be compared with the church of God there. You will say the same of the church of God at Corinth and the assembly of the people of Corinth, and, let us say, of the church of God at Alexandria and the assembly of the people of Alexandria. And if the one who hears this is fair-minded and examines the facts with a love of truth, he will marvel at him who both planned and was able to bring about the founding of churches of God everywhere, churches that live as sojourners beside the assemblies of the people in each city.

So too, if you compare the council of the church of God with the council in each city, you would find that some councillors of the church are worthy to hold citizenship in the city of God, if there is such a city anywhere in the universe, while the city councillors everywhere bring, in their own characters, nothing worthy of the pre-eminence their appointment gives them, by which they seem to stand above the citizens. So too the ruler of the church in each city must be compared with the ruler of the people in that city, so that you may perceive that, even among those councillors and rulers of the church of God who fall far short, and who live more carelessly than those of more vigorous life, it is nonetheless possible to find, as a general rule, a superiority in progress toward the virtues over the characters of those who sit as councillors and rulers in the cities.

title: Abaris’s arrow and Jesus taken up in glory
english: If this is so, is it not reasonable to think of Jesus, who has been able to establish so much, that no ordinary divinity was in him, but no longer reasonable to think so of Aristeas of Proconnesus, even if Apollo wishes to assign him a place among the gods, nor of those whom Celsus lists when he says, “No one thinks Abaris the Hyperborean a god, who had such power that he was carried along on an arrow”? For with what purpose did the divinity that let Abaris the Hyperborean be carried along on an arrow bestow so great a gift on him? So that the human race might be helped in some way? Or what did he himself gain by being carried along on an arrow? And this is even granting that these things are by no means fictions but came about through the cooperation of some demon.

But if my Jesus is said to have been taken up “in glory” (1 Timothy 3:16), I see the plan in it: the God who brought this about was commending the teacher to those who saw it, so that, as men contending not for human teachings but for divine teaching, they might devote themselves with all their strength to the God over all and do everything to please him, as those who would receive at the divine judgment seat, according to their deserts, whatever they had done in this life, whether good or evil (compare 2 Corinthians 5:10).

title: Jesus laid down his own soul
english: Next Celsus also spoke of the man of Clazomenae and, on the story told of him, added: “Do they not say this, that his soul often left his body and wandered about without a body? And men did not think him a god either.” To this too we shall say that perhaps some wicked demons arranged for such things to be written down (for I do not believe that they also arranged for them to happen), so that the things prophesied about Jesus and the things said by him might either be slandered as fictions like those, or not be greatly marvelled at, as having nothing more than the others.

Now my Jesus said of his own soul, which was parted from the body not by the necessity common to men but by the extraordinary authority given to him over this also: “No one takes my soul from me, but I lay it down of myself. I have authority to lay it down, and I have authority to take it again” (John 10:18). For since he had “authority to lay it down,” he laid it down when he said, “Father, why have you forsaken me?” (Matthew 27:46; Mark 15:34) and, “crying out with a loud voice, he gave up the spirit” (Matthew 27:50). In this he forestalled the executioners in charge of the crucified, who cut the legs of those crucified, and cut them for this reason, that they may not suffer punishment any longer (compare John 19:31–33).

And he took up “his soul” again when he showed himself to his disciples, having foretold it in their presence to the Jews who did not believe him: “Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up” (John 2:19). And “he was speaking of the temple of his body” (John 2:21). The prophets too had proclaimed such a thing beforehand in many places, and in this one: “Moreover my flesh also will dwell in hope; for you will not abandon my soul to Hades, nor will you let your Holy One see corruption” (Psalm 16:9–10; Acts 2:26–27).

title: Cleomedes and the chest
english: Celsus showed that he had read a good many Greek stories when he also cited the tale of Cleomedes of Astypalaea. He related that Cleomedes got into a chest and, though shut inside it, was not found within, but by some supernatural fate had flown out of it, when some men broke the chest open to seize him. If this too is a fiction, as it seems to be, it cannot be compared with the accounts of Jesus. For in the case of those men no token of the divinity reported of them is found in the life of men; but in the case of Jesus there are the churches of those who are helped, the prophecies spoken about him, the healings done in his name, and the knowledge joined with wisdom that comes from him, and the reasoned understanding found among those who have taken care to rise above bare faith and to search out the meaning in the divine Scriptures. They do this following the counsel of Jesus, who said, “Search the Scriptures” (John 5:39), and the wish of Paul, who taught that we must “know how to answer each one” as is fitting (Colossians 4:6), and of him also who said, “Always be ready to make a defence to everyone who asks you for a reason for the faith that is in you” (1 Peter 3:15).

But if Celsus wants it granted that the story is not a fiction, let him say for what purpose the power that is above man made Cleomedes fly out of the chest by some supernatural fate. For if he can present something worth mentioning, and show that a purpose worthy of God bestowed such a thing on Cleomedes, we shall judge what we ought to say in reply to him. But if he is at a loss to say anything even plausible on the point, then plainly, so far as no reason is to be found, we shall either discredit the story, siding with those who did not accept it, and charge it with being untrue, or we shall say that something demonic, like the illusions that sorcerers display by deceiving the eyes, did this also in the case of the man from Astypalaea, about whom Celsus supposes that an oracle declared that he had flown out of the chest by some supernatural fate.

title: We worship without temples or statues
english: For my part, I think that these were the only ones Celsus knew. And so that he may seem to have passed over similar cases by choice, he said, “And one could name many others of this kind.” Well, let it be so, and let it be granted that there have been many such men, who did nothing at all to help the human race. What would each of them be found to be when set beside the work of Jesus and the wonders told of him, of which we have spoken at length?

After this he supposes that we, in worshipping one who, as Celsus says, “was captured and died,” have done something like the Getae, who revere Zamolxis, the Cilicians, who revere Mopsus, the Acarnanians Amphilochus, the Thebans Amphiaraus, and the people of Lebadea Trophonius. Here too we shall prove that he had no good reason to liken us to those just named. For they built temples and statues to those whom he lists; but we have taken away from the Divine the honour paid by such means, as more fitting for demons, which are somehow settled in a particular place, a place they either seize beforehand or, drawn there by certain rites and sorceries, in a manner inhabit. We, rather, look with wonder on Jesus, who has turned our mind away from everything that the senses perceive, as being not only perishable but also bound to perish, and who leads it up to honour the God over all with an upright life and with prayers. These we offer to him through one who stands, as it were, between the nature of the uncreated and the nature of all created things, who brings us the benefits that come from the Father and, in the manner of a high priest, carries our prayers to the God over all.

title: If these are powers, Jesus is stronger
english: I should like to chat a little with the man who somehow says such things, in some such words as these, as befits him: Are these whom you have listed nothing, then? Is there no power at Lebadea connected with Trophonius, nor at Thebes around the temple of Amphiaraus, nor in Acarnania connected with Amphilochus, nor in Cilicia with Mopsus? Or is there in such places some being, whether a demon or a hero or even a god, working things greater than man can?

For if he says that there is nothing else about these, neither demonic nor divine, then let him at least now admit his own view as an Epicurean, one who does not think as the Greeks do, and who neither recognises demons nor even worships gods as the Greeks do. And let him be convicted of having brought forward to no purpose both what he said before, as though he accepted it as true, and what he goes on to add.

But if he says that those he lists are demons or heroes or even gods, let him see that by what he has said he will establish what he does not want: that Jesus too was something of this kind. That is why he has also been able to convince no small number of people that he came from God to dwell among the human race. And once Celsus admits this, see whether he will not be forced to say that Jesus is stronger than those with whom he has counted him. For none of those forbids the honours paid to the others; but Jesus, confident in himself as more powerful than all of them, forbids the acceptance of them as wicked demons, which have seized beforehand places on earth because they cannot touch the purer and more divine region, where the grossness that comes from the earth and from its countless evils does not reach.

title: Antinous is no match for Jesus
english: After this Celsus thinks that the story of Hadrian’s favourite (I mean the story of the youth Antinous, and the honours paid him by the people of the city of Antinous in Egypt) falls in no way short of the honour we pay to Jesus. Come, then, let us refute this too, as something said out of spite. For what has the life lived as the favourite of Hadrian, who did not even keep the male youth free from womanish disorder, in common with our revered Jesus? Even those who brought countless accusations against him and told every kind of lie about him have not been able to charge him with tasting even the least licentiousness, even for a short time.

Moreover, if anyone were to examine the facts about Antinous with a love of truth and without partiality, he would find that the sorceries and rites of the Egyptians are the causes of his seeming to do something in the city of Antinous even after his death. The same is reported to have been done in the case of other temples by Egyptians and by those skilled in such matters, who settle in certain places demons that give oracles or heal, and that often also torment those who seem to have transgressed in the matter of ordinary foods or of touching a dead human body, so that they may seem to strike fear into the uneducated multitude. Such too is the one who has come to be thought a god in the city of Antinous in Egypt. Some people, who live rather like cheats, invent false tales of his mighty deeds; others, deceived by the demon settled there, and others again, convicted by a weak conscience, suppose that they are paying a penalty sent by a god from Antinous. Such too are the mysteries they perform and their supposed oracles, from which the things of Jesus are very far removed.

For it was not sorcerers, coming together to repay a favour to some king who gave orders or some governor who commanded it, who were thought to have made him a god. It was the Maker of the universe himself who, in keeping with the marvellously persuasive power in his speaking, commended him as worthy of honour, not only to men who are willing to be of sound mind, but also to demons and other invisible powers. To this day these show either that they fear the name of Jesus as stronger than they, or that they reverently accept him as their lawful ruler. For if his commendation had not been given him by God, the demons too would not withdraw from those they assail, yielding at the mere pronouncing of his name.

title: Why Christians will not rank Jesus with Apollo or Zeus
english: The Egyptians, then, who have been taught to worship Antinous, will put up with it if you set Apollo or Zeus beside him, for they exalt Antinous by counting him among those gods. For here too Celsus plainly lies when he says, “Even if you set Apollo or Zeus beside him, they will not put up with it.”

But Christians have learned that their eternal life lies in knowing “the only true God,” who is over all, “and Jesus Christ, whom” he “has sent” (John 17:3). They have learned too “that all the gods of the nations are demons” (Psalm 96:5), greedy demons that wallow about the sacrifices, the blood, and the portions taken from the sacrifices, to deceive those who have not fled for refuge to the God who is over all; while the divine and holy angels of God are of another nature and another will than all the demons on earth, and are known to very few, to those who have searched into such things with understanding and care. If you set beside him Apollo and Zeus, or any of those worshipped with the savour of burnt fat, with blood, and with sacrifices, Christians will not put up with it. Some of them, in their great simplicity, do not know how to give an account of what they do, but sensibly keep what they have received. Others refuse with arguments that are not to be despised, arguments that are deeper and, as a Greek might say, esoteric and fit for those who have seen the higher mysteries. In these there is much discussion of God, and of those whom God, through the only-begotten God the Word, has honoured with a share in deity, and for that reason with the name as well. There is much discussion too of the divine angels, and of those who are opposed to the truth yet have themselves been deceived, and who out of that deception proclaim themselves gods, or angels of God, or good demons, or heroes formed by the change of a good human soul.

For just as many in philosophy suppose that they are in the truth, either because they have deceived themselves with plausible arguments or because they have rashly assented to arguments that others have put forward and devised, so too among souls outside bodies, and among angels and demons, there are some who have been drawn by plausible reasonings into proclaiming themselves gods. And because such questions cannot be found out among men with complete exactness, it has been judged safe for one who is a man to entrust himself to no one as to God except to the God who is over all alone, with Jesus Christ as arbiter, who looked most deeply into these things and handed them on to a few.

title: Lucky faith and tested faith
english: As for Antinous, then, or anyone else of the kind, whether among Egyptians or among Greeks, faith in him is, if I may use the word, unlucky. Faith in Jesus, however, is either one that might seem lucky, or one that has been examined under searching tests: to the many it seems lucky, while among a very few indeed it has been examined under searching tests. And even if I say that a certain faith is lucky, as the many would call it, I refer the question of this faith too to God, who knows the causes of what is allotted to each one who comes to live the life of men.

The Greeks too will say that even among those reckoned wisest, good fortune is in many respects the cause: for instance, in having teachers of a certain kind and in falling in with the better ones, when there are also teachers of the opposing schools, and in being brought up among better surroundings. For many have had an upbringing in such conditions that they were not allowed even to form an impression of better things, but always, from their earliest years, were either kept as the boy favourites of licentious men or masters, or held in some other wretchedness that keeps the soul from looking up. It is entirely likely that the causes of these things lie in the reasons of providence, but it is not easy for men to grasp them.

I have thought it right to say this in passing, by way of digression, because of how much faith of whatever kind achieves when it has taken hold beforehand. For because of men's different upbringings it was necessary to speak of the differences among their faiths, as they believe with better or with worse fortune; and from there to go on to the point that, even for the more able, what is called good fortune and what is called bad fortune would seem to contribute to their very appearing to be more rational, and to their attaching themselves, for the most part, more rationally to doctrines. But enough of these matters.

title: The plain honesty of the Gospel writers
english: We must now consider what Celsus says next. In it he says that with us too it is faith, having taken hold of our soul beforehand, that produces this kind of assent concerning Jesus. Faith does truly produce such assent in us. But see whether faith itself does not at once show what is praiseworthy in it, when we entrust ourselves to the God who is over all, giving thanks to the one who led us to such faith, and saying that it was not without God that he dared and achieved so great a thing.

We also trust the intentions of those who wrote the Gospels, discerning their reverence and their conscience, which show in their writings, for they have nothing spurious about them, nothing of the gambler's tricks, nothing made up and nothing crafty. For it is clear to us that souls which had not learned the sort of things taught by the crafty sophistry of the Greeks, which has great persuasiveness and sharpness, and by the rhetoric that wallows in the law courts, would not have been able to invent in this way matters that could carry in themselves what leads to faith and to a life in keeping with that faith.

I think too that this is why Jesus chose to use such men as teachers of his doctrine: so that there might be no room for any suspicion of plausible sophistries, and so that it might shine out plainly to those able to understand that the guilelessness of the writers' intention, which had in it much of what I may call simplicity, was counted worthy of a more divine power, a power that achieves far more than elaborate speech, the arrangement of words, and an argument that proceeds by divisions and the technical methods of the Greeks are thought able to achieve.

title: Common notions against idols
english: See whether the teachings of our faith, which from the first agree with the common notions, do not win over those who listen fair-mindedly to what is said. For even though perversion, with a great deal of instruction pleading its case, has been able to plant in the many the doctrine that statues are gods, and that things made of gold and silver and ivory and stone are worthy of worship, the common notion nevertheless requires us to understand that God is in no way perishable matter, and is not honoured when he is given shape by men in lifeless materials, as though these were made “in the image” of him (Genesis 1:26), or were some kind of symbol of him.

That is why it is said at once about statues “that they are not gods” (Acts 19:26), and about such works of craft that they bear no comparison with the Maker; and a few things are said about the God who is over all, who made, holds together, and governs the universe. And at once the rational soul, as though recognising what is akin to it, casts away what until then it had supposed to be gods, and takes up a natural love for its Creator. Through its love for him, it also welcomes with the warmest regard the one who first set these things before all the nations through the disciples he had trained, whom he sent out with divine power and authority to proclaim the word about God and his kingdom (Luke 9:1–2).

title: The Word and the change of his body
english: He charges us, I do not know how many times by now, about Jesus: that we consider him to be God although he was made of a mortal body, and that we think we act piously in this. It is needless to answer this any further, for more has been said above. Still, let those who make the charge know this. The one whom we consider and are persuaded to be from the beginning God and Son of God is the very Word (John 1:1), the very Wisdom (1 Corinthians 1:24), and the very Truth (John 14:6). As for his mortal body and the human soul in him, we say that through not only their fellowship with him but also their union and blending with him they have received what is greatest, and that, having shared in his divinity, they have been changed into God.

If anyone takes offence at our saying these things about his body as well, let him consider what the Greeks say about matter: that by its own definition it is without qualities, that it is clothed with whatever qualities the Maker wishes to put upon it, and that it often lays aside its former qualities and takes on better and different ones. If such views are sound, what is surprising in this, that by the providence of God, who willed it, the quality of mortality in the body of Jesus was changed into an ethereal and divine quality?

title: Perishable flesh and the gods of myth
english: It was not, then, as a trained reasoner that Celsus spoke when he compared the human flesh of Jesus with gold and silver and stone and said, “It is more perishable than these.” For in strict reasoning, neither is one imperishable thing more imperishable than another imperishable thing, nor one perishable thing more perishable than another perishable thing. But even granting that it is more perishable, we shall still say this in reply: if the matter that underlies all qualities can exchange its qualities, how can it not be possible for the flesh of Jesus also to exchange its qualities and become such as it had to be in order to dwell in the ether and the regions above it, no longer having the properties of fleshly weakness, nor the things that Celsus called “more foul”?

Nor in this does he act as a philosopher. For what is properly foul is such because of wickedness, and the nature of a body is not foul; for it is not insofar as it is the nature of a body that it has wickedness, which is what gives rise to foulness.

Then, since he foresees the defence we make about the change of his body, he says: “But once he has put these off, then, it seems, he will be a god. Why then not rather Asclepius, Dionysus, and Heracles?” We shall reply: What great deed did Asclepius or Dionysus or Heracles accomplish? And whom will they be able to show as improved in character and made better by their words and their life, so that they should become gods? Let us read the many stories about them and see whether they kept themselves clean of licentiousness, or injustice, or folly, or cowardice. If nothing of the kind were found in them, Celsus's argument in putting those just named on a level with Jesus would be strong. But if it is clear, even though some better things are reported of them, that they are recorded to have done countless things contrary to right reason, how can you still say with good reason that they, rather than Jesus, became gods when they put off the mortal body?

title: The tomb of Zeus in Crete
english: After this he says of us that we “laugh at those who worship Zeus, because his tomb is shown in Crete, and none the less revere the one from the tomb, not knowing how and in what sense the Cretans do such a thing.” Notice, then, that in these words he makes a defence for the Cretans, for Zeus and for his tomb, hinting at figurative meanings according to which the myth about Zeus is said to have been fashioned; but he accuses us, who admit that our Jesus was buried but declare that he was also raised from the tomb, which is something the Cretans do not go on to relate about Zeus.

Since he seems to plead for the tomb of Zeus in Crete when he says, “not knowing how and in what sense the Cretans do this,” we shall answer that even Callimachus of Cyrene, who read a vast number of poems and gathered up almost the whole of Greek history, knows of no figurative interpretation in the stories about Zeus and his tomb. That is why he reproaches the Cretans in the hymn he wrote to Zeus, saying: “Cretans are always liars; for the Cretans even built a tomb, O lord, for you; but you did not die, for you are for ever” (Callimachus, Hymn to Zeus 8–9).

Yet the man who said, “you did not die, for you are for ever,” while denying that Zeus was buried in Crete, records that the beginning of death came about for Zeus; for the beginning of death is birth upon earth. He speaks thus: “Among the Parrhasians Rhea lay down and bore you” (Callimachus, Hymn to Zeus 10). Since he denied the birth of Zeus in Crete because of his tomb, he ought to have seen that from his birth in Arcadia it followed that the one who had been born should also die. Callimachus also says this about these matters: “Zeus, some say you were born on the mountains of Ida; Zeus, others say in Arcadia. Which of them, father, have lied? Cretans are always liars” (Callimachus, Hymn to Zeus 6–8), and so on.

Celsus has led us into these matters by his unfairness about Jesus. He agrees with what is written, that he died and was buried, but he regards it as a fiction that he also rose from the dead, and this although countless prophets foretold this too, and there are many signs of his appearing after death.

title: The charge that Christians shun the educated
english: Next after this Celsus brings forward what is said, contrary to the teaching of Jesus, by a very few who are thought to be Christians, not, as he supposes, the more intelligent, but the most ignorant; and he says that they give orders such as these: “ ‘Let no one who is educated come near, no one wise, no one sensible; for these things are counted evil among us. But if anyone is ignorant, if anyone is foolish, if anyone is uneducated, if anyone is a child, let him come with confidence.’ For by admitting outright that these are worthy of their God, they make it plain that they wish to persuade, and are able to persuade, only the simple-minded, the low-born and the dull, slaves, silly women and little children.”

To this too we reply as follows. Suppose that, while Jesus teaches about self-control and says, “Whoever looks at a woman so as to desire her has already committed adultery with her in his heart” (Matthew 5:28), someone saw a few, out of so many who are thought to be Christians, living licentiously. He would be entirely reasonable in blaming them for living contrary to the teaching of Jesus, but he would act entirely unreasonably if he fastened the charge against them on the teaching itself. In the same way, if the teaching of Christians is found to summon people to wisdom as much as any other, then the blame must fall on those who plead in defence of their own ignorance, and who say, not the things Celsus recorded (for even if some are unlettered and ignorant, they do not speak so shamelessly), but other things, far milder, that turn people away from the pursuit of wisdom.

title: The ancient Scriptures call us to wisdom
english: That our teaching wants us to be wise must be shown both from the ancient Jewish writings, which we also use, and no less from those written after Jesus and believed in the churches to be divine. It is written in the fiftieth Psalm that David, in his prayer to God, says: “You have made plain to me the hidden and secret things of your wisdom” (Psalm 51:6). Indeed, anyone who reads the Psalms would find the book full of many wise doctrines. Solomon too was approved because he asked for wisdom (1 Kings 3:9–12; 2 Chronicles 1:10–12); and in his writings one can see the traces of his wisdom, which hold great depth of thought in few words. In them you would find many praises of wisdom and many exhortations to take up wisdom.

So wise indeed was Solomon that the queen of Sheba, when she heard “his name” “and the name of the Lord,” came “to test him with riddles” (1 Kings 10:1). She “spoke to him all that was in her heart, and Solomon explained to her all her words; there was not a word passed over by the king that he did not explain to her. And the queen of Sheba saw all the understanding of Solomon” (1 Kings 10:2–4) and all that belonged to him; “and she was beside herself, and she said to the king, ‘True was the report that I heard in my own land about you and about your understanding; and I did not believe those who told me until I came and my eyes had seen; and see, they did not tell me the half. You have added wisdom and good things to them beyond all the report that I heard’ ” (1 Kings 10:5–7).

It is written of him that “the Lord gave Solomon understanding and very great wisdom, and largeness of heart like the sand that is beside the sea. And wisdom was multiplied in Solomon exceedingly, beyond the understanding of all the ancients and beyond all the wise men of Egypt. And he was wiser than all men, and wiser than Gethan the Ezarite, and Emad, and Chalcadi, and Arada, the sons of Mad; and he was renowned among all the nations round about. And Solomon spoke three thousand parables, and his songs were five thousand. And he spoke of the trees, from the cedar that is in Lebanon to the hyssop that grows out through the wall; and he spoke of the fishes and the beasts. And all the peoples came to hear the wisdom of Solomon, and from all the kings of the earth, who heard of his wisdom” (1 Kings 4:29–34).

Our teaching so wants there to be wise men among believers that, to exercise the understanding of its hearers, it has spoken some things in riddles, some in what are called dark sayings (Proverbs 1:6), some through parables, and others through puzzles. And one of the prophets, Hosea, says at the end of his words: “Who is wise, and will understand these things? Or who is prudent, and will know them?” (Hosea 14:9). Daniel, and those who were taken captive with him, made such progress even in the learning practised in Babylon by the wise men around the king that they were shown to surpass them all “tenfold” (Daniel 1:20). And in Ezekiel it is said to the ruler of Tyre, who prided himself greatly on his wisdom: “Are you wiser than Daniel? Has not every secret been shown to you?” (Ezekiel 28:3).

title: Wisdom in the writings after Jesus
