english: If you go on to the books written after Jesus as well, you would find that the crowds of believers hear the parables as those who are outside (Mark 4:11) and worthy only of the outward teachings, while the disciples learn privately the explanations of the parables. For Jesus “privately explained everything to his own disciples” (Mark 4:34), honouring above the crowds those who laid claim to his wisdom. He promises to those who believe in him that he will send “wise men and scribes,” saying: “See, I will send you wise men and scribes, and some of them they will kill and crucify” (Matthew 23:34).

Paul too, in his list of the gifts given by God, placed first the word of wisdom; second, as ranking below it, the word of knowledge; and third, lower still, faith (1 Corinthians 12:8–9). And because he valued the word above miraculous workings, he therefore sets “workings of powers” and “gifts of healings” in a lower place than the gifts of the word (1 Corinthians 12:9–10).

Stephen, in the Acts of the Apostles, bears witness to the wide learning of Moses, no doubt taking this from ancient writings that had not reached many; for he says: “And Moses was instructed in all the wisdom of the Egyptians” (Acts 7:22). For this reason it was also suspected that he might be working his wonders not, as he professed, because he had come from God, but by the learning of the Egyptians, in which he was wise. For it was because he suspected something of this kind about him that the king called the enchanters of the Egyptians, and the wise men, and the sorcerers (Exodus 7:11); and they were proved to be nothing compared with the wisdom in Moses, which surpassed all the wisdom of the Egyptians.

title: Worldly wisdom and the wisdom of God
english: But it is likely that what Paul wrote in the First Letter to the Corinthians, addressed as it was to Greeks who were greatly puffed up over Greek wisdom, has moved some to think that our teaching does not want wise men. Let anyone who thinks so hear this. When the word censures worthless men, it says that they are not wise about things intelligible, invisible and eternal, but that, having busied themselves with the things of sense alone and placing everything in these, they are wise men of the world. In the same way, since there are many doctrines, it says that those which plead for matter and bodies, and assert that all things that primarily exist are bodies and that there is nothing else besides them, whether called invisible or named incorporeal, are “the wisdom of the world,” which is brought to nothing and made foolish, and the wisdom of this age (1 Corinthians 1:20; 2:6). But those which carry the soul over from the affairs of this world to the blessedness that is with God and to what is called his kingdom, and which teach people to despise all things perceived by sense and seen, as being temporary, and to hasten toward things invisible and to look at the things that are not seen (2 Corinthians 4:18), these it says are “the wisdom of God” (1 Corinthians 2:7).

Paul, as a lover of truth, says of certain wise men among the Greeks, in the points where they speak truly, “that, although they knew God, they did not glorify him as God or give thanks” (Romans 1:21). He bears witness that they had known God; and he says too that this did not come to them without God, where he writes: “for God has shown it to them” (Romans 1:19). He is hinting, I think, at those who ascend from things visible to things intelligible, when he writes that “the invisible things of God, from the creation of the world, are clearly seen, being understood through the things that are made, both his eternal power and divinity, so that they are without excuse, because, although they knew God, they did not glorify him as God or give thanks” (Romans 1:20–21).

title: Not many wise, but not none
english: Perhaps, too, some have been led by the words, “Consider your calling, brothers: not many were wise according to the flesh, not many powerful, not many of noble birth; but God chose the foolish things of the world to put the wise to shame; and God chose the low-born things and the despised things, and the things that are not, to bring to nothing the things that are, so that no flesh might boast before him” (1 Corinthians 1:26–29), to suppose that no one educated or wise or sensible comes to the word.

To such a person we shall reply that it does not say “no one wise according to the flesh,” but “not many wise according to the flesh.” And it is clear that when Paul, in his sketch of those called bishops, describes what kind of man the bishop must be, he also made him a teacher, saying that he must be able “also to refute those who contradict” (Titus 1:9), so that by the wisdom in him he may stop the mouths of empty talkers and deceivers (Titus 1:10–11). And just as for the office of bishop he prefers a man married once to one married twice, the “blameless” to the blameworthy, the “sober” to one who is not, the “self-controlled” to one who lacks self-control, and the “orderly” to one who is even slightly disorderly (1 Timothy 3:2), so he wants the man who is to be appointed bishop to be, above all, apt to teach (1 Timothy 3:2) and able “to refute those who contradict” (Titus 1:9).

How, then, can Celsus reasonably accuse us of saying, “Let no educated person come, no wise person, no sensible person”? No: let the educated, wise and sensible person come, whoever wishes; but let anyone who is ignorant, foolish, uneducated or childish come no less. For the word promises to heal such people too when they come, making all worthy of God.

title: Education is no barrier to knowing God
english: It is false, too, that those who teach the divine word wish to persuade only “the silly, the low-born, the dull, slaves, women and little children.” The word does call these, to make them better; but it also calls those who are far above them, since Christ is “the Saviour of all men, and especially of believers” (1 Timothy 4:10), whether intelligent or simpler, and he is “the propitiation” “with the Father” “for our sins, and not for ours only but also for the whole world” (1 John 2:1–2).

After this, then, it is needless for us to want to defend ourselves against Celsus’s words, which run thus: “For what evil is there, in any case, in being educated, in having devoted oneself to the best teachings, and in being sensible and seeming so? What hindrance is this to knowing God? Why is it not rather a help, and a means by which one might better reach the truth?”

To be truly educated, then, is no evil, for education is a road to virtue. Yet not even the wise men of the Greeks will say that those who hold mistaken doctrines should be counted among the educated. Again, who would not agree that it is good to have devoted oneself to the best teachings? But which shall we call the best teachings, if not those that are true and summon us to virtue? Being sensible is also a fine thing, but not merely seeming so, which is what Celsus said. Being educated, having devoted oneself to the best teachings, and being sensible do not hinder the knowledge of God; they even help toward it. And it is more fitting for us to say this than for Celsus, especially if he is shown to be an Epicurean.

title: Christians are not market-place charlatans
english: Let us look also at what follows in his text, which runs thus: “But surely we see, too, that those who put on the most disreputable displays in the market-places and go round collecting would never come forward into a gathering of sensible men, nor dare to put on their own show among them; but wherever they see adolescents, a crowd of house-slaves and a throng of foolish people, there they push their way in and preen themselves.”

See how he slanders us here as well, likening us to those who put on the most disreputable displays in the market-places and go round collecting. What are these most disreputable displays of ours? Or what do we do that resembles theirs, we who, through readings and through expositions of the readings, urge people to piety toward the God of the universe and to the virtues that share its throne, and turn them away from contempt for the divine and from everything done against right reason?

Philosophers, indeed, would pray to collect so many hearers for discourses that summon them to what is good; and this is what some of the Cynics in particular have done, conversing in public with whoever happens to be passing. Will they say, then, that these men too, who do not gather those thought to be educated but call hearers from the crossroads and bring them together, are like those who put on the most disreputable displays in the market-places and go round collecting? Yet neither Celsus nor anyone who thinks as he does finds fault with those who, out of what they regard as love for humanity, address their discourses even to the common, uneducated people.

title: How Christians test and admit their hearers
english: If those men are not to blame for doing this, let us see whether Christians do not summon the crowds to goodness and nobility of character even more, and better, than they do. For the philosophers who converse in public do not sort out their hearers: whoever wishes stands and listens. Christians, on the other hand, first test, as far as they can, the souls of those who wish to hear them, and first instruct them privately; then, when the hearers seem, before entering the common assembly, to have made enough progress toward the will to live well, they bring them in. They form a separate class of those who are just beginning and being introduced and have not yet received the sign of their cleansing, and another of those who have shown, as far as they can, that their purpose is to want nothing other than what Christians hold. Among them certain persons are appointed to inquire into the lives and conduct of those who come forward, so that they may bar from their common assembly those who do disreputable things, while those who are not such they welcome with their whole soul and make better day by day.

And what a discipline they keep toward those who sin, especially the licentious, whom they drive out of the community, these people who, according to Celsus, are like those who put on the most disreputable displays in the market-places! The revered school of the Pythagoreans used to build cenotaphs for those who fell away from their philosophy, reckoning that they had become dead men. But Christians mourn as dead those who have been overcome by licentiousness or some other outrage, as men lost and dead to God. And if they show a change worth noting, they receive them back later, as men risen from the dead, after a longer time than is required of those being introduced at the start; but those who have fallen after coming to the word they do not enroll in any office or position of leadership in what is called the church of God.

title: Deeper teaching kept for able hearers
english: Consider, then, what Celsus says next, “Surely we see, too, those who put on the most disreputable displays in the market-places and go round collecting,” and see whether it is not said with plain falsehood and by a comparison that does not fit. Of these people to whom Celsus likens us, those who put on the most disreputable displays in the market-places and go round collecting, he says that they would never come forward into a gathering of sensible men, nor dare to put on their own show among them, but that wherever they see adolescents, a crowd of house-slaves and a throng of foolish people, there they push their way in and preen themselves. In saying this he does nothing but abuse us, like the women at the crossroads whose aim is to speak ill of one another.

For we do everything in our power so that our gathering may be made up of sensible men; and we venture to bring into the open what is finest and most divine among us in our discourses to the assembly at those times when we have plenty of intelligent hearers. But we conceal the deeper things and pass them over in silence when we see that those who come together are simpler and need teachings figuratively called “milk” (1 Corinthians 3:2).

title: Milk for beginners, solid food for the mature
english: For our Paul, writing to the Corinthians, who were Greeks but not yet cleansed in their ways, says: “I gave you milk to drink, not solid food, for you were not yet able to take it. Indeed, even now you are still not able, for you are still fleshly. For where there is jealousy and strife among you, are you not fleshly, and walking in a merely human way?” (1 Corinthians 3:2–3). The same man, knowing that some things are food for a more mature soul, while the teachings for beginners are likened to the milk of infants, says: “And you have come to need milk, not solid food. For everyone who lives on milk is unskilled in the word of righteousness, for he is an infant. But solid food belongs to the mature, to those whose faculties have been trained by practice to distinguish good from evil” (Hebrews 5:12–14).

Would those, then, who believe that these words are well spoken suppose that what is fine in the word would never be spoken in a gathering of sensible men, but that wherever they see adolescents, a crowd of house-slaves and a throng of foolish people, there they bring the divine and sacred things into the open and preen themselves on them before such people? No: it is plain to anyone who examines the whole intent of our writings that Celsus, hating the Christian race just as the uneducated common people do, says such things without examination, and falsely.

title: The word invites the foolish to wisdom
english: We admit that we want to educate everyone with the word of God, even if Celsus does not wish it, so as to give adolescents too the encouragement that suits them, and to show house-slaves how, by taking on a free spirit, they may be made noble by the word. Those among us who champion Christianity say plainly enough that they are debtors “to Greeks and barbarians, to the wise and the foolish” (Romans 1:14). For they do not deny that they must heal the souls of the foolish too, so that, as far as possible, they may lay aside their ignorance and hasten toward greater understanding. They hear Solomon also when he says, “And you who are foolish, apply your heart” (Proverbs 8:5), and, “Whoever of you is most foolish, let him turn aside to me; and to those who lack sense I, Wisdom, give this charge, saying: Come, eat my bread, and drink the wine I have mixed for you; forsake folly, that you may live, and set your understanding straight in knowledge” (Proverbs 9:4–6).

I would also say this, in view of the charges in Celsus’s argument: Do not those who practise philosophy invite adolescents to hear them? Do they not call young men who have lived the worst of lives to better things? And do they not want house-slaves to practise philosophy? Or are we too to accuse philosophers of turning house-slaves toward virtue: Pythagoras, who turned Zamolxis; Zeno, who turned Persaeus; and, only the other day, those who turned Epictetus toward philosophy? Or is it allowed to you Greeks to call adolescents, house-slaves and foolish people to philosophy, while we, when we do this, do not do it out of love for humanity, though we wish to heal every rational nature with the medicine of the word and to bring it into kinship with God, who made all things?
This, then, would be enough in answer to Celsus’s abuse, for it is abuse rather than accusation.

title: Celsus paints Christians as household workmen
english: Since, taking pleasure in his account of insults against us, he has added still other things, come, let us set these out as well and see whether it is the Christians who disgrace themselves, or Celsus by what he says. He says: “We see, too, in private houses, wool-workers and cobblers and fullers and the most uneducated and boorish people, who do not dare to utter a word in front of their older and wiser masters; but whenever they get hold of the children privately, and some foolish women along with them, they pour out some astonishing things: that the children must not heed their father and their teachers, but must obey them; that the father and teachers talk nonsense and are senseless, and neither know nor can do anything truly good, their minds already taken up with empty chatter; but that they alone know how one ought to live, and if the children obey them, they will be blessed and will make their home happy.

“And if, while they are speaking, they see one of the schoolteachers coming by, or someone wiser, or even the father himself, the more cautious of them scatter in fright, while the bolder egg the children on to throw off the reins, whispering such things as this: that while the father and the teachers are present they will be neither willing nor able to explain anything good to the children, for they shrink from the stupidity and coarseness of those men, who are utterly corrupt, far gone in wickedness, and who punish them; but if the children wish, they must leave their father and their teachers and go with the women and their little playmates to the women’s quarters, or the cobbler’s shop, or the fuller’s shop, so that they may receive perfection. And by saying these things they win them over.”

title: What we really teach women and boys
english: See, then, in this passage too, how he mocks those among us who teach the word and try in every way to raise the soul up to the Creator of the universe, who show that one must despise all things that are perceived by the senses, temporary and seen (compare 2 Corinthians 4:18), and must do everything in order to attain fellowship with God, the contemplation of things intelligible and invisible, and a blessed life with God and with those who belong to God; and how he compares them to the wool-workers in houses, and to the cobblers and fullers and the most boorish of men, as men who invite children, mere infants, and women to base things, so that they will abandon father and teachers and follow them.

From what sober-minded father, or from what teachers of nobler things, do we draw away children and women? Let Celsus show it; and in the case of the children and women who come to our teaching, let him set side by side and compare whether any of the things they used to hear was better than ours, and in what way we draw children and women away from fine and noble studies and invite them to worse ones. But he will not be able to show any such thing against us. On the contrary, we draw women away from licentiousness and from the perversion that comes from their companions, and from all mad love of theatres and dancing, and from superstition; and the boys who are just reaching manhood and swelling with sexual desires we bring to self-control, setting before them not only the shamefulness that lies in these sins, but also the state in which the soul of the wicked will be because of such things, what penalties it will pay, and how it will be punished.

title: Which teachers talk nonsense?
english: And which are the teachers we say talk nonsense and are senseless, the ones Celsus stands up for as teaching better things? Unless perhaps he thinks that those who invite women to superstition and to licentious spectacles are good teachers of women and do not talk nonsense, and also that those are not senseless who lead the young and drive them along toward all the disorderly things that we know are done by them in many places.

We, for our part, invite even those who come from the doctrines of the philosophers, as far as we can, to our worship of God, showing how excellent and pure it is. But since by what he said Celsus has made out that we do not do this, but call only the foolish, we would say to him: If you were charging us with drawing away from philosophy those already devoted to it, you would not be speaking the truth, though your argument would have some plausibility. But as it is, since you say that we draw those who come to us away from good teachers, show us teachers other than the teachers of philosophy, or those who have devoted themselves to some useful subject. But he will have nothing of the kind to show.

We do promise, openly and not in secret, that those will be blessed who live according to the word of God, who look to him in all things, and who carry out whatever they do as in the sight of God who watches them. Are these, then, the lessons of wool-workers and cobblers and fullers and the most uneducated rustics? But he will not be able to show it.

title: Before good fathers we speak freely
english: But the people Celsus describes, who resemble the wool-workers in houses and are like the cobblers and fullers and the most uneducated rustics, “while the father and teachers are present,” he says, “will be neither willing to say anything nor able to explain anything good to the children.” To this too we shall reply: What sort of father do you mean, sir, and what sort of teacher? If one who welcomes virtue, turns away from vice and embraces what is better, then hear this: we shall speak our teaching to the children with great confidence, as men who stand well with such a judge. But if, in front of a father notorious for his opposition to virtue and nobility of character, and in front of those who teach things contrary to sound reason, we keep silent, do not blame us for this either, for you have no good reason to blame us.

You yourself, at any rate, when you hand on the sacred rites of philosophy to young men and sons whose fathers consider philosophy an idle and useless thing, will not speak to the boys in front of their worthless fathers; rather, wishing to separate from their wicked fathers the sons who have been drawn toward philosophy, you will watch for opportunities so that the words of philosophy may reach the young.

We shall say the same about the teachers as well. If we turn the young away from teachers who teach the indecencies of comedy, and licentious iambic verse, and whatever else neither reforms the speaker nor benefits hearers who do not know how to listen to poems as philosophers do and to pick out from each what tends to the benefit of the young, then in doing this we are not ashamed to admit what we do. But if you show me teachers who train the young beforehand for philosophy and exercise them in philosophy, I shall not turn the young away from them. Rather, once they have been trained beforehand, as it were, in the general course of studies and in philosophical reasoning, I shall try to lead them up to the majestic and lofty eloquence of Christians, hidden from the many, who discuss the greatest and most necessary matters, and who demonstrate and show that these were treated philosophically by the prophets of God and the apostles of Jesus.

title: First healing, then the mysteries
english: Then after this Celsus, aware that he has abused us rather too bitterly, says, as though defending himself: “That I am making no harsher accusation than the truth compels, let anyone judge from the following as well. Those who summon people to the other rites of initiation proclaim beforehand: ‘Whoever has clean hands and intelligent speech’; and others again: ‘Whoever is pure from every defilement, whose soul is conscious of no evil, and who has lived well and justly.’ These are the proclamations of those who promise purification from sins. But let us hear whom these people summon. ‘Whoever is a sinner,’ they say, ‘whoever is without understanding, whoever is a child, and, in a word, whoever is wretched, him the kingdom of God will receive.’ Do you not mean by ‘the sinner’ the unjust man, the thief, the housebreaker, the poisoner, the temple-robber and the grave-robber? Whom else would a robber summon by public proclamation?”

To this we reply that it is not the same thing to call those who are sick in soul to healing, and those who are healthy to the knowledge and understanding of diviner things. We know both of these. At the beginning, when we invite people to be healed, we urge sinners to come to the teachings that teach them not to sin, those without understanding to the teachings that produce understanding, children to rise in mind to manhood, and, in a word, the wretched to happiness, or, to use the more proper word, to blessedness. But when those among them who are making progress show that they have been cleansed by the Word and, as far as they can, have lived a better life, then we call them to our own rites of initiation, for “we speak wisdom among the perfect” (1 Corinthians 2:6).

title: Who may come to the Christian mysteries
english: And since we teach that “wisdom will not enter a soul that plots evil, nor dwell in a body in debt to sin” (Wisdom of Solomon 1:4), we say: Whoever has clean hands, and for that reason lifts up “holy hands” (1 Timothy 2:8) to God, and, because he performs lofty and heavenly deeds, can say, “The lifting up of my hands is an evening sacrifice” (Psalm 141:2), let him come to us. And whoever has intelligent speech, because he meditates on the law of the Lord “day and night” (Psalm 1:2), and because he has “faculties trained by practice to distinguish good and evil” (Hebrews 5:14), let him not hesitate to come to solid food for the mind (Hebrews 5:14), food fit for athletes of piety and of every virtue.

And since “the grace” of God is “with all who love” the Teacher of the lessons of immortality “in incorruption” (Ephesians 6:24), whoever is pure not only from every defilement but also from the sins that are thought to be lesser, let him with confidence be initiated into the mysteries of the worship of God taught by Jesus, mysteries that are rightly handed on only to the holy and pure.

Celsus’s man of the mysteries, then, says: “Let him come whose soul is conscious of no evil.” But the one who, following Jesus, leads initiates to God will say to those who have been purified in soul: He whose soul has for a long time been conscious of no evil, and especially since he came to the healing of the Word, let him hear also the things that Jesus spoke in private to his true disciples (compare Mark 4:34). So, in setting the practice of those who initiate people among the Greeks against those who teach the doctrine of Jesus, Celsus does not know the difference between the wicked, who are called to healing, and those already most pure, who are called to the deeper mysteries.

title: A different calling from the robber’s
english: It is not, then, to the mysteries and to a share in the wisdom hidden “in a mystery,” “which God foreordained before the ages for the glory” of his righteous ones (1 Corinthians 2:7), that we call the unjust man, the thief, the housebreaker, the poisoner, the temple-robber, the grave-robber, and whatever others Celsus might name in his exaggeration; we call them to healing. For in the divinity of the Word there are, on the one hand, healing remedies for those who are “sick,” about whom the Word said: “Those who are well have no need of a physician, but those who are sick” (Matthew 9:12; Mark 2:17). And there are, on the other, remedies that show to those who are pure in soul and body “the revelation of the mystery that was kept in silence through eternal ages, but is now made manifest through the prophetic writings” (Romans 16:25–26) and through “the appearing of our Lord Jesus Christ” (1 Timothy 6:14; compare 2 Timothy 1:10), an appearing that shines upon each of the perfect and enlightens the ruling part of the soul for an unerring knowledge of things as they are.

But since, exaggerating his charges against us, he adds to those whom he named among the foulest of men the words, “Whom else would a robber summon by public proclamation?”, we shall reply to this as well: A robber calls such people in order to use their wickedness against those whom he wishes to murder and rob. But a Christian, even if he calls those whom the robber calls, calls them with a different calling, so that he may bind up “their wounds” with the Word (Luke 10:34) and pour on the soul inflamed with evils the remedies that come from the Word, which answer to the wine and oil and poultice and the other aids of the medicine of the soul.

title: The physician sent to sinners
english: Next he misrepresents what has been said and written to exhort those who have lived badly, calling them to repentance (Luke 5:32) and to the reform of their souls, and he says that we claim God was sent to sinners. In this too he acts like someone who would find fault with people for saying that a most humane king had sent the physician because of those in the city who were in a bad way. So God the Word was sent: as physician to sinners (Matthew 9:12), and as teacher of divine mysteries to those who are already pure and no longer sin.

Celsus could not tell these apart, for he did not care to learn, and he says: "Why was he not sent to those without sin? What evil is it not to have sinned?" To this we say that if by "those without sin" he means those who no longer sin, then our Saviour Jesus was sent to them too, though not as a physician. But if he means those who have never sinned at all (for he made no distinction in his wording), we shall say that no human being can be without sin in that sense. We say this while making an exception of the man understood in Jesus, "who committed no sin" (1 Peter 2:22).

Celsus speaks maliciously about us, as though we claimed that "God will receive the unjust man if he humbles himself because of his wickedness, but will not receive the just man if he looks up to him with virtue from the beginning." We say that it is impossible for a human being to look up to God with virtue from the beginning. For evil must first exist in human beings, as Paul too says: "When the commandment came, sin came to life again, and I died" (Romans 7:9-10). Nor do we teach about the unjust man that it is enough for him to humble himself because of his wickedness in order to be received by God. Rather, if he condemns himself for his former deeds and walks "humble" over them, and "well ordered" in his later conduct (Plato, Laws 716a), God will accept him.

title: Humbling oneself before God is not flattery
english: Then, not understanding the sense in which it is said, "Everyone who exalts himself will be humbled" (Luke 14:11; Luke 18:14), not having learned even from Plato that the noble and good man walks "humble and well ordered" (Plato, Laws 716a), and not knowing either that we say, "Humble yourselves, therefore, under the mighty hand of God, that he may exalt you in due time" (1 Peter 5:6), he says that "men who rightly preside over justice stop those who lament over their crimes from making piteous, wailing speeches, so that they may not be judged by pity rather than by truth; but God, it seems, judges not by truth but by flattery."

Yet what flattery, what piteous and wailing speech, takes place according to the divine Scriptures when the sinner says in his prayers to God: "I made my sin known, and I did not hide my lawlessness; I said, I will confess my lawlessness against myself to the Lord" (Psalm 32:5), and the words that follow? Or can he show that such conduct on the part of sinners, when they humble themselves under God in their prayers, does not help to convert them?

Confused by his eagerness to accuse, he contradicts himself. In one place he implies that he knows a man who is without sin and just, who looks up to God with virtue from the beginning; in another he accepts what we say: "What man is perfectly just, or who is without sin?" For he speaks as one who accepts it: "This is fairly true, that the human race is somehow by nature inclined to sin." Then, as though not everyone were called by the word, he says: "So one ought simply to have called everyone, if indeed all sin."

Yet we showed earlier that Jesus said: "Come, all you who labour and are burdened, and I will give you rest" (Matthew 11:28). All human beings, then, "labouring and burdened" because of the nature of sin, are called to the rest that is found with the Word of God. For God sent forth "his Word, and healed them, and rescued them from their corruptions" (Psalm 107:20).

title: The tax collector and the Pharisee
english: He also says: "What, then, can this preference for sinners be?" and adds other things of the same kind. We shall answer that, taken absolutely, a sinner is not preferred to one who is not a sinner. But sometimes a sinner who is aware of his own sin, and for that reason goes on to repentance, humble over what he has done wrong, is preferred to one who is thought to be less of a sinner but does not consider himself a sinner; instead he exalts himself over certain better qualities that he believes he finds in himself, and is puffed up about them.

For those willing to read the Gospels fairly, this is made plain by the parable about the tax collector who said, "Be merciful to me, the sinner" (Luke 18:13), and about the Pharisee who boasted with a kind of wicked conceit and said, "I thank you that I am not like the rest of men, robbers, unjust, adulterers, or even like this tax collector" (Luke 18:11). For Jesus adds to his account of both: "This man went down to his house justified rather than the other; for everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, and everyone who humbles himself will be exalted" (Luke 18:14).

So we do not blaspheme God, nor lie about him, when we teach every person, whoever he may be, to be aware of human smallness compared with the majesty of God, and always to ask of him what our nature lacks, since he alone is able to supply what is wanting in us.

title: Who comes to the faith, and why
english: He supposes that we say such things to exhort sinners because we are unable to win over any man who is truly good and just, and that for this reason we open our gates to the most unholy and abandoned. But if anyone would consider our assembly fairly, we can point to more who have turned from a life that was not very bad than who have turned from the most abandoned sins.

For those who are conscious of better things in themselves, and who pray that what is preached about God's reward to the better may be true, are naturally readier to assent to what is said than those who have lived very wickedly. These are kept by their very conscience from accepting that they will be punished by the Judge of all with a punishment that would befit one who has sinned so greatly, and that the Judge of all would inflict without going against right reason. Sometimes, too, even if the utterly abandoned wish to accept the teaching about punishment because of the hope set on repentance, they are held back by their habit of sinning. Long steeped in it, and stained fast by vice, as it were, they can no longer easily turn away from it to a settled life, a life according to right reason.

Celsus too grasped this, I do not know how, and in what follows he says: "And yet it is surely plain to everyone that no one could completely change those who are naturally inclined to sin and accustomed to it, not even by punishing them, much less by showing mercy. For to change nature completely is exceedingly hard. But those without sin are better partners in life."

title: Philosophers too know that people can change
english: Here too Celsus seems to me badly mistaken, in not allowing complete change to those naturally inclined to sin and accustomed to doing it, since he thinks that they are not healed even by punishments. For it is plain that all of us human beings are naturally inclined to sin, and some are not only inclined to sin but also accustomed to it; yet not all human beings are incapable of complete change. For in every school of philosophy, and in the divine word as well, there are men recorded to have changed so much that they are held up as a pattern of the best life. Some cite, among the heroes, Heracles and Odysseus; among later men, Socrates; and among those of very recent times, Musonius.

So Celsus spoke falsely, not only by our account, when he said that it is plain to everyone that those naturally inclined to sin and accustomed to it could not be brought by anyone, not even under punishment, to a complete change for the better. He spoke falsely also by the account of those who have practised philosophy nobly and have not despaired that it is possible for human beings to take up virtue. But even if he did not set out precisely what he meant, we shall nonetheless give him a fair hearing, and even so we shall show that he does not speak soundly. For he said: "No one could completely change those who are naturally inclined to sin and accustomed to it, not even by punishing them"; and we have overturned, as best we could, the sense his words plainly give.

title: Phaedo and Polemo
english: It is likely that he means something like this: that no one could completely change, not even by punishing them, those who are not only naturally inclined but also accustomed to sins of this kind, the sort committed by the most abandoned. This too is shown to be false from the history of certain men who became philosophers. For who would not rank among the most abandoned the man who somehow brought himself to submit to a master who put him in a brothel, so that he would receive anyone who wished to shame him? Such things are told of Phaedo. And who will not say that the vilest of all men was the one who burst into the school of the most venerable Xenocrates with a flute-girl and a band of revellers who shared his debauchery, to insult a man whom even his companions admired?

Yet teaching had the power to turn even these men and to make them advance so far in philosophy that the one was judged by Plato worthy to recount Socrates' discourse on immortality and to portray his steadfastness in prison: how he paid no heed to the hemlock, but fearlessly, with complete calm of soul, discussed matters so many and so great that even those who are thoroughly composed and troubled by no circumstance can hardly follow them; and the other, Polemo, turning from a profligate into a man of the greatest self-control, succeeded to the school of Xenocrates, a man renowned for his dignity. So Celsus does not speak the truth when he says that no one could completely change those who are naturally inclined to sin and accustomed to it, not even by punishing them.

title: The power of the apostles’ words
english: Still, that the order, composition and style of philosophical discourses should have done such things for the men just named and for others who had lived badly is not very surprising. But when we consider the words that Celsus calls unlearned, filled with power as though they were charms, and observe those words urging whole multitudes at once to pass from licentiousness to the steadiest of lives, from injustice to a better life, and from cowardice or unmanliness to such firmness that they despise even death because of the piety that has shown itself in them, how shall we not rightly marvel at the power within it?

For "the word" of those who first served as ambassadors of these things and laboured to found churches of God, and their "preaching" as well, came with persuasion, but not the kind of persuasion found in those who profess the wisdom of Plato or of any other philosopher, men who had nothing beyond human nature. But the demonstration given by God in the apostles of Jesus was persuasive, coming "from the Spirit and power" (1 Corinthians 2:4). That is why their word, or rather the Word of God, ran with the utmost speed and keenness, changing through them many of those naturally inclined to sin and accustomed to it. No human being could have changed them, not even by punishing them; but the Word remade them, forming and shaping them according to his own will.

title: Changing a nature grown evil
english: Celsus, drawing the consequence of his own view, says: “To change a nature completely is exceedingly hard.” But we know that every rational soul has one nature, and we hold that none was fashioned evil by the Creator of all things, but that many have become evil through their upbringing, through perversion and through the talk that surrounds them, so that in some people evil has even become second nature. And we are persuaded that for the divine Word to change an evil that has become second nature is not only not impossible but not even very hard, provided only that a person accepts that he must entrust himself to the God over all and do everything with a view to pleasing him. With him it is not true that “the base and the noble are held in one honour,” nor that “the idle man and the man who has done much die alike” (Homer, Iliad 9.319–320).

And if for some people change is very hard indeed, the cause must be said to lie in their assent, which shrinks from accepting that the God over all is a just judge of each person for all that he has done in life. For choice and training have great power even over things that seem hardest and, to speak in hyperbole, all but impossible. Or is it the case that human nature, when it has resolved to walk on a rope stretched high in the air across the middle of the theatre, and to carry so many and such heavy weights while doing it, has been able by training and attention to accomplish such a feat, but when it resolves to live by virtue it is incapable, even if it had formerly become utterly base? Consider whether the man who says such things is not finding fault with the nature that made the rational creature rather than with the creature that was made, if it has made human nature capable of things so hard and of no use whatever, but incapable of reaching its own blessedness. But this too is enough in answer to “For to change a nature completely is exceedingly hard.”

Next he says: “Those who are without sin are better companions in life.” He does not make clear whom he calls sinless, whether those who were so from the beginning or those who became so by a change. Those who were so from the beginning cannot exist; those who became so by a change are rarely found, and they become such through having come to the saving Word. They do not come to the Word already being such; for without the Word, and the perfect Word at that, it is impossible for a man to become sinless.

title: What God can and cannot do
english: Then he raises an objection, as though we said it: “God will be able to do all things.” He does not even see how this is said, what “all things” are included in it, or how God is able. There is no need to speak of these matters now; for he himself did not take a stand against the saying, though he could have done so plausibly. Perhaps he did not follow the plausible case that could be made against it, or he followed it but also saw the reply to that argument. In our view God can do all things that he can do without departing from being God, from being good and from being wise.

But Celsus, as one who has not understood how God is said to be able to do all things, says: “He will not wish anything unjust,” granting that he can do even what is unjust, but does not wish to. We say that, just as what sweetens by nature, because it is sweet, cannot make things bitter against the one cause by which alone it acts, and what gives light by nature, because it is light, cannot make things dark, so neither can God do injustice; for the power to do injustice is contrary to his deity and to all the power that accords with it. And if any being can do injustice because its nature is fitted for injustice as well, it can do injustice since it does not have in its nature the inability ever to do injustice.

title: Whom God relieves and accepts
english: After this he takes for granted what is not conceded by those who believe more rationally, though it is perhaps held by some foolish people: that God, like those who are slaves to pity, is a slave to pity for those who wail, and so relieves the wicked, while he casts away the good who do nothing of the sort, which is most unjust. For in our view God does not relieve any wicked man who has not yet turned to virtue, and he casts away no one who is already good; nor does he relieve anyone who wails, or show him mercy, to use “mercy” in its more ordinary sense, on account of his wailing.

But those who have condemned themselves severely for their sins, so that on this account they mourn and lament for themselves, as it were, as lost, so far as their past deeds go, and who show a notable change, God accepts for the sake of their repentance; so too those who have changed from a most wicked life. For virtue grants such people an amnesty, when it comes to dwell in their souls and has cast out the evil that had seized them before. And even if it is not virtue but notable progress that arises in the soul, this too is enough, in proportion to how far the progress goes, to cast out and blot out the flood of evil, so that it is almost no longer found in the soul.

title: True wisdom does not lead astray
english: Then, as though speaking in the person of the one who teaches our doctrine, he says: “For the wise turn away from what we say, led astray and hampered by their wisdom.” To this too we shall reply: if wisdom is knowledge of things “divine and human” and of their causes, or, as the divine word defines it, “a breath of the power of God and a pure emanation of the glory of the Almighty” (Wisdom of Solomon 7:25), and “a radiance of eternal light, a spotless mirror of the working of God, and an image of his goodness” (Wisdom of Solomon 7:26), then no one who is wise would turn away from what is said by a Christian who has knowledge of Christianity, nor would he be led astray or hampered by wisdom. For it is not true wisdom that leads astray, but ignorance; and of all that exists only knowledge is firm, and truth; and these come from wisdom.

But if, departing from the definition of wisdom, you call wise the man who lays down any doctrine whatever with the help of certain sophisms, we shall say that the man who is wise by what you call wisdom does indeed turn away from the words of God, led astray by plausible arguments and sophisms and hampered by them. And since, as our teaching says, “wisdom is not knowledge of wickedness” (Sirach 19:22), and “knowledge of wickedness,” if I may call it so, is found in those who hold false opinions and are deceived by petty sophisms, I would therefore call it ignorance rather than wisdom in such people.

title: Lawgivers and the unschooled crowd
english: After this he again abuses the man who champions Christianity, and pronounces that he recounts laughable things, but he does not prove, or even clearly set out, the things he calls laughable. In his abuse he says that no sensible man is persuaded by the teaching, being misled himself by the great number of those who come to it. In this too he acts like a man who would say, because of the great number of unschooled people who are guided by the laws, that no sensible man obeys, let us say, Solon or Lycurgus or Zaleucus or any of the others, and especially if he takes “sensible” to mean the man whose character is shaped by virtue. For just as with such people the lawgivers, according to what seemed useful to them, put them under such a discipline and such laws, so God, giving laws in Jesus to men everywhere, guides even those who are not sensible, so far as such people can be guided toward the better.

The God who speaks in Moses knew this, as we have also said above, and says: “They moved me to jealousy with what is no god; they provoked me to anger with their idols; and I will move them to jealousy with what is no nation; with a senseless nation I will provoke them to anger” (Deuteronomy 32:21). Knowing it, Paul too said: “God chose the foolish things of the world to put the wise to shame” (1 Corinthians 1:27). By “the wise” he means, in a broad sense, all who seem to have advanced in learning but have fallen away into godless polytheism, since “claiming to be wise, they became fools, and exchanged the glory of the incorruptible God for the likeness of an image of corruptible man and birds and four-footed beasts and creeping things” (Romans 1:22–23).

title: Seeking the foolish and the clever
english: He also charges the teacher with seeking out the foolish. To him we would say: Whom do you call foolish? For strictly speaking every base man is foolish. If, then, you call the base foolish: when you bring men to philosophy, do you seek to bring the base or the worthy? It cannot be the worthy, for they have already become philosophers. The base, then; and if the base, the foolish. And you seek to bring many such men to philosophy; so you too seek the foolish. As for me, even if I seek those who are called foolish in this sense, I do the same as a humane physician would if he sought out the sick in order to bring them remedies and make them strong.

But if you call foolish those who are not quick-witted but the more grotesque among men, I will answer you that I try to improve these too as far as I can, but it is not from these that I wish to form the assembly of Christians. For I rather seek the more quick-witted and sharper, since they can follow the explanation of the riddles and of the things said in a hidden way in the Law and the Prophets and the Gospels. These you have despised as containing nothing worth mention, without having examined the meaning in them or tried to enter into the intention of those who wrote them.

title: Which physicians do we turn people from?
english: After this he says that the man who teaches the things of Christianity acts much like one who promises to make bodies well, yet turns people away from heeding skilled physicians, because they would expose his own lack of skill. To this too we shall reply: Which physicians do you mean, from whom we turn away the unlearned? For you surely do not suppose that we bring our call to the word to people who study philosophy, so that you might take them to be the physicians from whom we turn away those we summon to the divine word. Either, then, he gives no answer, since he cannot name the physicians, or he must fall back on the unlearned, who themselves go about repeating like slaves what is said of many gods and whatever else the unlearned might say. Either way he will be shown to have brought into his argument, to no purpose, the man who turns people away from skilled physicians.

And even supposing that we turn away from the philosophy of Epicurus, and from the physicians reckoned Epicureans after Epicurus, those who have been deceived by them, how shall we not be acting with the best of reason when we draw them away from a grievous disease which the physicians of Celsus have put into them, the disease of doing away with providence and bringing in pleasure as a good? Or let it be granted that we draw those whom we urge toward our word away from other physicians, philosophers of the Peripatetic school, who do away with providence toward us and with the relation of the divine to human beings. How shall we not make those we have converted godly, and heal them, by persuading them to devote themselves to the God who is over all, and free those who listen to us from great wounds, the wounds that come from the arguments of so-called philosophers?

Let it be granted too that we turn others away from Stoic physicians, who bring in a God who can perish and say that His substance is a body that can be changed throughout, altered and transformed, and who at some time destroy all things and leave God alone. How shall we not, in this case also, free from evils those who listen to us, and bring them to the godly doctrine that teaches them to devote themselves to the Creator and to marvel at the father of the Christian teaching, who out of the greatest love for mankind arranged for teachings that turn souls back to be sown throughout the whole human race? And if we heal those who have caught the folly of transmigration from physicians who bring the rational nature down, sometimes into any irrational nature at all, and sometimes even into a nature without sense-impressions, how shall we not make better in soul those who listen to a doctrine that does not teach that the wicked man is given insensibility or irrationality as his share of punishment, but shows that the pains and punishments God brings on the wicked are remedies meant to turn them back? For Christians who live wisely guide the simpler ones with this in mind, as fathers guide their very little children.

We do not, then, turn to children and foolish rustics and say to them, “Flee the physicians.” Nor do we say, “Take care that none of you ever lays hold of knowledge.” Nor do we assert that knowledge is an evil, nor are we so mad as to say that knowledge leads people astray from health of soul. Nor would we ever say that anyone perishes from wisdom, we who do not say even when we teach, “Attend to me,” but, “Attend to the God of the universe, and to Jesus, the teacher of the lessons about Him.” None of us is such a braggart as to say to his disciples what Celsus put into the mouth of the teacher: “I alone will save you.” See, then, how many lies he tells about us. Nor do we say that the true physicians destroy those they promise to heal.

title: Who is really drunk
english: He also brings a second comparison against us, saying that our teacher acts as if a drunkard went in among drunkards and accused the sober of being drunk. Then let him show from the writings, say, of Paul, that the apostle of Jesus was drunk and that his words were not sober; or from what John wrote, that his thoughts do not breathe the spirit of a man of sound mind, free from the drunkenness that comes from vice. No one, then, who is of sound mind and teaches the Christian doctrine is drunk; rather, Celsus says this as he reviles us in a way unworthy of a philosopher.

And let Celsus say which sober people we who uphold the doctrines of the Christians accuse. For in our view all who speak to lifeless things as to a god are drunk (Wisdom of Solomon 13:17). And why do I say drunk? Rather they are mad, who hurry to the temples and bow down to statues or animals as gods. And no less mad than these are those who think that things made by common craftsmen, and at times by the most worthless of men, have been fashioned to honour true gods.

title: Who is really blind
english: After this he likens the teacher to a man with diseased eyes and the learners to people with diseased eyes, and says that this man, among those whose eyes are diseased, charges the keen-sighted with being blind. Which Greeks, then, would we say do not see, in our view, if not those who, from the vast magnitude of the things in the world and the beauty of what has been created (Wisdom of Solomon 13:5), cannot look up and see that one must worship, admire and revere Him alone who made these things, and that nothing made by human beings and used in honour of gods could rightly be revered, whether apart from God the Creator or together with Him? For to compare things that admit of no comparison at all with the infinite One, who surpasses all created nature beyond measure, is the work of those whose minds are blind.

We do not, then, say that the keen-sighted have diseased eyes or are blind. Rather we declare that those who, in ignorance of God, wallow in temples and statues and what are called holy festivals have been blinded in mind; above all when, besides their impiety, they also live in licentiousness, not even seeking what deed might be honourable, but doing everything that deserves shame.

title: Not the wicked but the simple
english: After charging us with so much, he wants to make it plain that he has other things he could say but passes them over in silence. His words run thus: “These things and the like I find fault with, so as not to list them all; and I say that they do wrong in insulting God, in order to lead on wicked men with empty hopes and persuade them to despise better things, on the ground that if they keep away from them it will be better for them.”

To this one might reply, from what actually happens among those who come to Christianity, that it is not so much the wicked who are led on by the word as the simpler sort and, as most people would call them, the unpolished. For these people, through fear of the punishments that are proclaimed, a fear which moves them and urges them to keep away from the things that bring punishment, try to give themselves to the worship of God that Christianity teaches. And the word so masters them that, through fear of what the word calls eternal punishments (Matthew 25:46), they despise every torment men devise against them, and death with countless pains. No one of sound mind would say that this is the work of wicked choices.

How can self-control and chastity, or generosity and readiness to share, be practised out of a wicked choice? Nor can the fear of God spring from such a choice, the fear to which the word, as something useful for the many, calls those who cannot yet see what is to be chosen for its own sake and choose it as the greatest good, above every promise. From all this it follows that such things do not by nature arise in one who chooses to live in wickedness.

title: The best laws the many could bear
english: But suppose someone imagines that, in these matters, it is superstition rather than wickedness that marks most of those who believe the word, and he charges our word with making people superstitious. We shall say to him that one of the lawgivers, when asked whether he had laid down the best laws for his citizens, replied, “Not the best absolutely, but the best of those they could receive” (Plutarch, Life of Solon 15). So too the father of the Christian doctrine might say: “I have laid down the best laws and teaching that the many could receive for the improvement of their character. I threaten sinners with pains and punishments that are not false, but true and necessary, and brought to bear for the correction of those who resist, even though they do not wholly understand the purpose of the one who punishes, or what the pains are meant to do.” For this too is spoken for their benefit, both in keeping with the truth and, to good purpose, with something held back.

Yet, on the whole, those who uphold the teachings of Christianity do not lead on the wicked. Nor do we insult the divine. For what we say about it is true; and to the many it seems clear, though it is not as clear to them as it is to the few who give themselves to studying the things of the word with philosophy.

title: Empty hopes and the philosophers
english: Celsus also says that those who become Christians are led on by empty hopes. Since he thus finds fault with the doctrine of the blessed life and of fellowship with the divine, we shall say to him: By your reasoning, sir, those also who have accepted the teaching of Pythagoras and Plato about the soul are led on by empty hopes, the teaching that the soul is by nature able to rise to the vault of heaven and, in the place above the heavens, to behold the sights that the blessed spectators see (Plato, Phaedrus 247b–c). By your account, Celsus, those too who have accepted that the soul survives, and who live so as to become heroes and to spend their days with the gods, are led on by empty hopes. And perhaps those persuaded that the mind which comes “from outside” (Aristotle, Generation of Animals 736b) is immortal, and will continue its life as mind, might also be said by Celsus to be led on by empty hopes.

Let him, then, no longer hide his own school, but confess that he is an Epicurean, and do battle against what Greeks and barbarians have said, in terms far from contemptible, about the immortality of the soul, or its survival, or the immortality of the mind. Let him show that these are arguments that deceive with empty hopes those who assent to them, while the arguments of his own philosophy are free of empty hopes, and either lead to good hopes or, what better fits his position, instil no hope at all, since the soul is at once utterly destroyed. Unless, indeed, Celsus and the Epicureans will deny that their own hope is empty, the hope about their end, pleasure, which on their view is the good: “the stable condition of the flesh,” and the expectation of it which Epicurus holds sure (Epicurus, fragment 68 Usener).

title: Nothing better than trust in God
english: Do not suppose that, in a way unfitting for the Christian doctrine, I have brought in against Celsus those who have taught philosophy on the immortality or the survival of the soul. Since we share some things with them, we shall find it easier to show that the blessed life to come will belong only to those who have accepted the worship of God that Jesus teaches, and a devotion to the Creator of the universe that is sincere and pure and unmixed with anything at all that is created.

Let anyone who wishes show which better things we persuade people to despise. Let him set against one another, on the one side, the blessed end that we teach, an end with God in Christ, that is, in the Word and Wisdom (1 Corinthians 1:24, 30) and all virtue, which will come to those who have lived blamelessly and purely and have taken up an undivided and unbroken love for the God of the universe, and will meet them as the gift of God; and on the other side, the end set forth by each philosophical school among Greeks or barbarians, or promised by a mystery. Let him show that the end held by one of the others is better than ours, and that it holds together as true, while ours befits neither the gift of God nor those who have lived well; or that these things were not spoken by the divine Spirit who filled the souls of the pure prophets. Let anyone who wishes show that words admitted by all to be human are better than words shown to be divine and proclaimed by divine inspiration.

And what better things do we teach those who accept our word that they will do better to be rid of? If it is not too bold to say so, it is plain at once that nothing can be conceived as better than to entrust oneself to the God who is over all, and to give oneself to a teaching that draws a person away from everything created and brings him, through the Word, who is animate and living, who is also living Wisdom and the Son of God, to the God who is over all.

But since the third book of what we have dictated against the treatise of Celsus has now reached a sufficient length with these words, we shall bring our discourse to a close here, and in the books that follow we shall contend against what Celsus wrote next.
